posts.post_title: True Statements About Cage Layer Fatigue
posts.post_content: Which of the following statements is true about Cage Layer Fatigue?

_aimcq_options.text: It is a type of osteoporosis commonly found in layers in the cage system
It is caused by excess calcium and phosphorus in the diet

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above (three correct sub-statements from original)

All three original sub-statements about Cage Layer Fatigue are correct:

  1. It is a type of osteoporosis, commonly found in layers kept in the cage system.
  2. It is due to deficiencies of calcium, phosphorus, and Vitamin D (not excess — the correct sub-statement says deficiency).
  3. Lack of exercise may contribute to the disease, as birds in cages cannot move freely.
Cage Layer Fatigue — Details
  • Syndrome: Metabolic bone disease (osteoporosis) in commercial layers in battery cages.
  • Primary cause: Calcium depletion from bones to support intensive egg shell formation, combined with inadequate dietary Ca, P, and Vit. D.
  • Aggravating factor: Inability to exercise in cages → muscles weaken → birds cannot stand.
  • Signs: Inability to stand, paralysis of legs, thin fragile bones.
  • Prevention: Adequate Ca (3–3.5%), P (0.65%), and Vit. D₃ in feed; ensure adequate light for Vit. D synthesis.
Why Other Options Are Wrong (individual options)
  • Excess Ca/P → incorrect; it is DEFICIENCY that causes cage layer fatigue.
  • Exercise prevents entirely → exercise helps, but dietary correction is also essential.

posts.post_title: False Statement About Tibial Dyschondroplasia
posts.post_content: Which of the following statements about Tibial Dyschondroplasia is NOT true?

_aimcq_options.text: It is a leg disorder in broilers
It is a leg disorder in layers
Abnormal formation of cartilage in leg bones is involved
High dietary level of chloride may increase incidence

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer (NOT TRUE): It is a leg disorder in layers

Tibial Dyschondroplasia (TD) is a leg disorder in BROILERS, NOT layers. It occurs due to abnormal cartilage formation in the proximal tibia (tibiotarsus), leading to lame birds and economic losses in broiler production.

Tibial Dyschondroplasia — Key Facts
  • Affects: Primarily fast-growing broilers (not layers).
  • Lesion: Abnormal, non-vascularised plug of cartilage in the growth plate of the tibia.
  • Predisposing factors: Rapid growth, high dietary chloride, dietary cation-anion imbalance, deficiencies of Vit. D, Ca, or P.
  • Clinical signs: Leg weakness, lameness, swollen hock joints.
Leg Problems in Poultry — Summary

Tibial DyschondroplasiaBroilersAbnormal cartilage; high Cl diet
Perosis (Slipped tendon)BothMn, Biotin, Choline, Folic acid deficiency
Cage Layer FatigueLayersCa, P, Vit. D deficiency + no exercise

posts.post_title: Hormone Responsible for Broodiness in Poultry
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for broodiness in poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Prolactin

Prolactin (from the anterior pituitary) is the hormone responsible for broodiness in poultry. It triggers the broody behaviour (sitting on eggs, aggression, cessation of laying) in hens.

Broodiness in Poultry
  • Broodiness is the external manifestation of the maternal instinct to incubate eggs.
  • It is a dominant sex-linked character.
  • Good layers (e.g., Leghorn) are less broody; poor layers are more broody.
  • Broodiness causes a complete cessation of egg laying — an economically undesirable trait in commercial layers.
Key Hormones in Poultry Reproduction
HormoneFunction
ProlactinBroodiness (maternal incubation behaviour) ✔
Vasotocin (AVT)Oviposition (contraction of uterus to expel egg)
LHTriggers ovulation
FSHFollicle development on ovary
OestrogenMedullary bone calcium mobilization for shell
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Growth hormone → promotes body growth; not linked to broodiness.
  • Vasotocin → responsible for oviposition (egg expulsion), not broodiness.
  • Oxytocin → uterine contraction in mammals; in poultry, vasotocin plays this role.

posts.post_title: Hormone Responsible for Oviposition in Poultry
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for oviposition (egg laying/expulsion) in poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vasotocin (AVT — Arginine Vasotocin)

Arginine Vasotocin (AVT), also called Vasotocin, is a hormone secreted from the posterior pituitary in birds. It causes contraction of the uterus (shell gland), resulting in oviposition — the process of laying the egg.

Vasotocin vs. Oxytocin
  • Vasotocin (AVT) is the avian equivalent of Oxytocin in mammals.
  • Oxytocin causes uterine contractions and milk let-down in mammals (cows, sheep).
  • Vasotocin causes uterine (shell gland) contraction and oviposition in birds.
Complete Reproductive Hormone Summary for Poultry
HormoneSourceFunction
FSHAnterior pituitaryFollicle development
LHAnterior pituitaryOvulation trigger
ProlactinAnterior pituitaryBroodiness
Vasotocin (AVT)Posterior pituitaryOviposition (uterine contraction)
OestrogenOvarySecondary sex characters; Ca mobilization
ProgesteroneOvaryLH surge; oviduct function
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Prolactin → responsible for broodiness, not oviposition.
  • Growth hormone → promotes growth; unrelated to oviposition.
  • Oxytocin → the mammalian equivalent; in birds, Vasotocin performs this role.

posts.post_title: Optimum Egg-Shell Thickness
posts.post_content: Optimum egg-shell thickness should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 0.30–0.50 mm

The optimum egg-shell thickness for a standard chicken egg is 0.30–0.50 mm. Shell thickness is directly proportional to shell strength and is measured using a Screw gauge.

Egg Shell Composition
  • Eggshell contributes 11% of total egg weight (along with shell membranes).
  • Inorganic matter: 96% (94% CaCO₃ + 1% MgCO₃ + 1% Ca₃(PO₄)₂)
  • Organic matter: 4%
Shell Thickness vs. Shell Strength
  • Shell strength is directly proportional to shell thickness.
  • Thin shells result from calcium deficiency in the feed, leading to soft-shelled eggs.
  • For best hatching results, optimum shell thickness should be 0.33 mm.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 0.10–0.20 mm → too thin; would represent a very fragile, deficient shell.
  • 0.30 µm → micrometres are 1000× smaller than mm; this would be microscopically thin and impossible.
  • 0.50 nm → nanometres are 1,000,000× smaller than mm; biologically meaningless for shell thickness.

posts.post_title: Example of Pellet Binder in Poultry Feed
posts.post_content: Which of the following is an example of a pellet binder used in poultry feed?

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Molasses, Sodium bentonite, and Guar meal)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

Molasses, Sodium bentonite (clay), and Guar meal are all examples of pellet binders used in poultry feed manufacturing.

What Are Pellet Binders?
  • Pellet binders are additives that help the feed ingredients hold together when compressed into pellets.
  • Without binders, pellets may crumble easily (high fines), wasting feed and reducing palatability.
Common Pellet Binders and Their Properties
BinderSource/Nature

MolassesBy-product of sugar industry; sticky liquid

  • Flavouring agents: Poultry nectar
  • Pellet binders: Sodium bentonite, Molasses, Guar meal ✔

posts.post_title: Live Culture of Useful Bacteria in Animal Feed
posts.post_content: A live culture of useful bacteria added to animal feed is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Probiotics

Probiotics are defined as live cultures of beneficial (useful) bacteria that, when fed in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host. Common probiotic strains used in poultry are Lactobacillus and Streptococcus species.

Probiotics vs. Prebiotics vs. Antibiotics
TermDefinitionExample
ProbioticsLive beneficial bacteria culturesLactobacillus acidophilus, L. bulgaricus
PrebioticsNon-digestible feed ingredients that stimulate growth of beneficial gut bacteriaFOS (Fructooligosaccharides), Inulin
AntibioticsCompounds produced by microorganisms that inhibit/kill bacteriaPenicillin, Tetracycline, Bacitracin
SynbioticsCombination of probiotics + prebiotics—
Benefits of Probiotics in Poultry
  • Competitive exclusion of pathogenic bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter).
  • Improved intestinal villi height and nutrient absorption.
  • Enhanced immune response.
  • Reduced need for antibiotic growth promoters.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Antibiotics → kill/inhibit bacteria; they are not live cultures themselves.
  • Enzymes → biological catalysts (e.g., beta-glucanase, phytase); not live bacteria.
  • Prebiotics → non-digestible carbohydrates that feed beneficial bacteria; not themselves live cultures.

posts.post_title: CO₂ Level in Incubator That Causes 100% Embryo Death
posts.post_content: During incubation, if the CO₂ concentration in the incubator rises above ______%, all embryos die and hatchability becomes zero:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5%

If the CO₂ level in the incubator rises above 5% for a prolonged period, all embryos die and hatchability becomes zero.

CO₂ Effects on Hatchability
  • Optimum CO₂ level: 0.5%
  • For every 1% rise in CO₂ beyond 0.5% → embryonic mortality rises progressively.
  • Above 5% CO₂ → all embryos die → hatchability = 0%.
O₂ Effects on Hatchability
  • Optimum O₂ level: 21%
  • For every 1% fall in O₂ from 21% → hatchability drops by 5%.
  • For every 1% rise in O₂ from 21% → hatchability rises by 5%.
Ventilation Problems and Their Consequences
  • Poor ventilation → accumulation of CO₂ and NH₃, wet litter, dead embryos.
  • CO₂ > 5% is directly lethal to embryos.
  • NH₃ maximum permissible in poultry house: 25 ppm.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 1% → causes elevated embryonic mortality but not complete death.
  • 3% → causes significant mortality but hatchability is not zero yet.
  • 10% → too high an estimate; lethality occurs at 5%.

posts.post_title: Singing Time for Poultry Carcass Processing
posts.post_content: The singing time for poultry (passing carcass over blue flame to burn hair-like appendages) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5–10 seconds over blue flame

Singing is the process of passing the plucked poultry carcass over a blue flame for 5–10 seconds to burn off the tiny, hair-like feather appendages (filoplumes) that remain after de-feathering.

Singing vs. Scalding — Key Differences
ProcessPurposeMethod
ScaldingLoosen feathers for pluckingImmersion in hot water (58–60°C / 1 min)
SingingBurn residual hair-like appendagesBlue flame, 5–10 seconds
Why Blue Flame?
  • A blue flame (complete combustion) is hotter and cleaner than a yellow/orange flame.
  • It burns the fine filoplumes quickly without scorching the skin.
  • 5–10 seconds is sufficient; longer exposure would burn or discolour the carcass skin.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 10–20 seconds → too long; risks burning and discolouring the skin.
  • 20–25 seconds → excessively long; would damage the carcass.

posts.post_title: Method to Determine Specific Gravity of Egg
posts.post_content: The specific gravity of an egg is determined by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Brine floatation technique

The specific gravity of an egg is determined by the Brine flotation technique. The egg is placed in solutions of salt (brine) of known specific gravity; the specific gravity at which the egg just floats indicates its own specific gravity.

Specific Gravity of Standard Egg
  • Specific gravity range of fresh egg: 1.060–1.090
  • Higher specific gravity = thicker shell = better egg quality.
  • As an egg ages, specific gravity decreases (air cell enlarges, moisture and CO₂ are lost).
Summary of Egg Quality Measurement Tools
ParameterMeasurement Tool
Albumin quality (Haugh unit)Haugh unit meter (measures albumin height)
Yolk quality (Yolk index)Yolk height / Yolk width ratio
Egg shape index (ESI)Vernier caliper
Shell strength / thicknessScrew gauge
Specific gravityBrine flotation technique
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Vernier caliper → used for egg shape index (ESI), not specific gravity.
  • Screw gauge → used for shell thickness/strength, not specific gravity.

posts.post_title: Instrument Used to Measure Egg Shell Strength
posts.post_content: Egg Shape Index (ESI) of an egg is measured by Vernier caliper, while shell strength is measured by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Screw gauge

Shell strength (and shell thickness) are measured using a Screw gauge. Shell strength is directly proportional to shell thickness.

Vernier Caliper vs. Screw Gauge
  • Vernier caliper: Measures external dimensions with accuracy of 0.1 mm → used for ESI (egg length and width).
  • Screw gauge (micrometer screw gauge): Measures much smaller distances with accuracy of 0.01 mm → used for shell thickness (0.30–0.50 mm).
ESI Formula

ESI = (Maximum width / Maximum length) × 100

  • ESI of chicken egg: 74
  • ESI of duck egg: 72
  • ESI of quail egg: 78
  • High ESI = more rounded egg; Low ESI = more elongated egg.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Vernier caliper → used for ESI, not shell strength.
  • Brine flotation → used for specific gravity, not shell strength.
  • Micrometer → although similar to screw gauge, the standard term used is 'Screw gauge' in poultry science.

posts.post_title: Egg Shape Index of Chicken Egg
posts.post_content: The Egg Shape Index (ESI) of a chicken egg is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 74

The Egg Shape Index (ESI) of a standard chicken egg is 74. ESI represents the ratio of maximum width to maximum length of the egg, expressed as a percentage.

ESI Formula

ESI = (Maximum width / Maximum length) × 100

ESI of Different Poultry Species
SpeciesESI
Chicken74
Duck72
Japanese Quail78
Interpretation of ESI
  • Higher ESI (e.g., 78–80) → more rounded egg shape.
  • Lower ESI (e.g., 68–70) → more elongated egg shape.
  • Ideal ESI for hatching: close to 74 for chicken (neither too round nor too elongated).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 72 → ESI of duck egg, not chicken.
  • 76, 80 → higher than the standard chicken ESI of 74.

posts.post_title: Interpretation of Egg Shape Index (ESI)
posts.post_content: A higher Egg Shape Index (ESI) indicates a ______ egg shape, while a lower ESI indicates a ______ egg shape:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rounded, Elongated

ESI = (Width / Length) × 100. A higher ESI means the width is relatively large compared to the length, indicating a rounder egg. A lower ESI means the egg is narrower relative to its length, making it more elongated.

Practical Example
  • If an egg has width = 40 mm and length = 54 mm → ESI = (40/54) × 100 = 74 → standard chicken egg shape.
  • If ESI = 80 → width/length ratio is higher → rounder egg.
  • If ESI = 65 → width/length ratio is lower → elongated egg.
ESI Across Species
SpeciesESIShape
Duck72Slightly elongated
Chicken74Standard oval
Quail78Slightly rounder
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Elongated, Rounded → reverse of the correct interpretation.
  • Elliptical, Circular / Circular, Elliptical → these are not the standard terms used for ESI interpretation.

posts.post_title: Functional Ovary in Adult Chicken
posts.post_content: In adult chicken, which ovary/oviduct is functional?

_aimcq_options.text: Neither ovary is functional outside breeding season

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Only left ovary is functional

In adult poultry (hen), only the left ovary and left oviduct remain functional. At birth, both ovaries and oviducts are present, but the right ovary and right oviduct regress and atrophy during development.

Why Only the Left Ovary?
  • This is an evolutionary adaptation — having two functional ovaries simultaneously could cause problems with the large egg-laying process.
  • The right ovary typically regresses during embryonic development, and only the left persists in most birds.
  • In some raptors (hawks, falcons), both ovaries may be functional.
Shape and Appearance of the Active Ovary
  • Active ovary in poultry resembles a bunch of grapes due to the multiple follicles (developing yolks) at various stages of maturation.
  • A typical laying hen has 5–6 large yellow follicles plus numerous smaller ones.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Only right ovary → incorrect; it is always the left in domestic fowl.
  • Both functional → correct only in a few raptor species; not in domestic fowl.

posts.post_title: Shape of Active Ovary in Poultry
posts.post_content: The shape of the active ovary in poultry resembles:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bunch of grapes

The active (functional) ovary in a laying hen resembles a bunch of grapes because of the numerous follicles (each containing a developing yolk) at various stages of maturation clustered together.

Ovarian Follicle Hierarchy
  • A mature laying hen's ovary contains follicles at many stages: large yellow follicles (F1, F2, F3, F4, F5) and many smaller white follicles.
  • F1 (largest, ~35 mm) is about to ovulate.
  • One follicle ovulates approximately every 24–26 hours in a productive layer.
Comparison with Other Species
  • Cattle ovary: Almond-shaped, smooth surface.
  • Sheep/Goat ovary: Small, almond-shaped.
  • Poultry ovary: Bunch of grapes (due to multiple visible surface follicles).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Almond shape → describes the ovary of cattle and small ruminants.
  • Bean shape → not a standard description for any domestic species' ovary.
  • Cauliflower shape → may describe pathological ovarian tumours; not the normal ovary.

posts.post_title: Viral Diseases of Poultry
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a viral disease of poultry?

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Ranikhet, Gumboro, and Marek's disease)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

Ranikhet disease, Gumboro disease, and Marek's disease are all important viral diseases of poultry.

Summary of Key Poultry Viral Diseases
DiseaseCausative AgentKey Feature
Ranikhet (Newcastle Disease)ParamyxovirusRespiratory + nervous signs; vaccination mandatory
Gumboro (IBD)BirnavirusBursa of Fabricius destruction; immunosuppression
Marek's DiseaseHerpesvirus (HVT)Lymphoma; paralysis; vaccination at day 1
Fowl PoxPoxvirusSkin lesions or diphtheritic membrane
Infectious Bronchitis (IB)CoronavirusRespiratory and reproductive lesions
Standard Broiler Vaccination Schedule

Broilers are vaccinated against exactly three diseases: Marek's disease, Gumboro (IBD), and Ranikhet (Newcastle Disease).

  • Marek's disease + Debeaking: Day 1 (hatchery)
  • Gumboro (IBD): 14th day
  • Ranikhet (F1 strain): 21st day
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Any single option alone is incomplete since all three are viral diseases.

posts.post_title: Cause of Encephalomalacia (Crazy Chick Disease) in Poultry
posts.post_content: Encephalomalacia (Crazy Chick Disease) in poultry is caused due to deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vitamin E

Encephalomalacia (Crazy Chick Disease) is caused by Vitamin E deficiency. It is characterised by softening of the cerebellum due to oxidative damage, leading to incoordination, falling over, and 'crazy' movements in chicks.

Vitamin E Functions in Poultry
  • Potent antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage (peroxidation of unsaturated fatty acids).
  • Works synergistically with Selenium (Se).
  • Essential for normal reproductive function in breeders.
Vitamin E Deficiency Conditions in Poultry
  • Encephalomalacia (Crazy chick disease): Cerebellar softening; incoordination.
  • Exudative diathesis: (with Se deficiency) — subcutaneous oedema due to capillary permeability increase.
  • Muscular dystrophy (White muscle disease): (with Se deficiency) — degenerative changes in muscles.
Complete Vitamin Deficiency Disease List for Poultry
  • Vit. B₁ (Thiamine): Polyneuritis (star-gazing)
  • Vit. B₂ (Riboflavin): Curled toe paralysis
  • Vit. E: Encephalomalacia / Crazy chick disease ✔
  • Biotin: Fatty Liver Kidney Syndrome (FLKS)

posts.post_title: Feeding Method with Maximum Selective Feeding Risk
posts.post_content: Chances of selective feeding are maximum in which method of poultry feeding?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Whole grain feeding

Selective feeding is maximum in the whole grain feeding method because birds can pick and choose specific grain types (e.g., preferring maize over soya, or wheat over sorghum), leading to nutritional imbalance.

Comparison of Feeding Methods
MethodSelective Feeding RiskNotes
Whole grain feedingMaximumBirds choose preferred grains; nutritional imbalance possible
Grain + mash feedingModerateSlightly better than whole grain
All mash feedingMinimum / NoneBest method; prevents selective feeding
Pellet feedingMinimumAll nutrients compacted; minimises waste; 10% costlier
Crumble feedingLowBroken pellets; used for chicks
Best Commercial Feeding Method

All mash feeding is the best method for commercial poultry production to avoid selective feeding. When a question asks to 'avoid selective feeding' → answer is All mash; when it asks 'maximum selective feeding' → answer is Whole grain feeding.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • All mash feeding → prevents selective feeding (minimum risk).
  • Pellet feeding → pellets contain all nutrients in each bite; minimal selection possible.

posts.post_title: Location of Air Cell in Chicken Egg
posts.post_content: The air cell of a chicken egg is situated at the:

_aimcq_options.text: On the side of the egg depending on position at laying

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Broad end of egg

The air cell is the space between the inner and outer shell membranes and is always located at the broad end of the chicken egg.

Why the Air Cell Is at the Broad End
  • The broad end contains the maximum number of pores for gaseous exchange.
  • After the egg is laid and cools down, the contents contract slightly, creating the air cell at the broad end.
  • The embryo's head develops towards the broad end during incubation so it can use the air cell oxygen for the first breath before pipping.
Air Cell Size as a Quality Indicator
  • Freshly laid egg: Air cell depth = 1–3 mm (very small).
  • As the egg ages, the air cell enlarges due to evaporation of water and loss of CO₂.
  • A large air cell = old egg.
  • Air cell depth measured in specific gravity or brine flotation gives freshness index.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Narrow end → where the pointed end is; no air cell here.
  • Middle → not anatomically possible; air cell is always at broad end.
  • Side of egg → air cell location is fixed, not variable.

posts.post_title: Maximum Aflatoxin B₁ Limit in Broiler and Layer Feed
posts.post_content: The maximum limit of Aflatoxin B₁ (ppb) permitted in both broiler and layer feed is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 20 ppb

As per BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) 2007, the maximum permissible limit of Aflatoxin B₁ in both broiler and layer feed is 20 ppb (parts per billion).

What is Aflatoxin B₁?
  • Produced by the fungus Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus, particularly in stored maize, groundnut cake, and cottonseed cake under warm, humid conditions.
  • Aflatoxin B₁ is the most potent naturally occurring carcinogen known.
  • In poultry, it causes Aflatoxicosis: reduced feed intake, poor growth, immunosuppression, liver damage, and reduced egg production.
BIS Aflatoxin Limits Across Feed Types
  • All poultry feeds (broiler pre-starter to layer phase II): 20 ppb Aflatoxin B₁ maximum.
Related Fungal Diseases in Poultry
  • Aspergillosis (Brooder pneumonia): Caused by Aspergillus fumigatus; respiratory disease in young chicks from contaminated litter/hatchery environment.
  • Aflatoxicosis: Caused by dietary Aflatoxin B₁ > 20 ppb (from Aspergillus flavus/parasiticus in mouldy feed).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 10 ppb → more restrictive than BIS specification.
  • 15 ppb → not the BIS-specified limit.
  • 50 ppb → excessively permissive; beyond safe limits.

posts.post_title: True Statements About Chicken Egg Structure
posts.post_content: Which of the following is true about the chicken egg?

_aimcq_options.text: The embryo head forms toward the broad end because maximum pores for gaseous exchange are at the broad end
The air cell is located at the narrow end of the egg
The depth of air cell in freshly laid egg is 5–7 mm

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Embryo head forms toward the broad end because maximum pores are there

All three facts about the chicken egg are correct:

  1. The embryo head forms toward the broad end because the maximum number of pores (for O₂ intake and CO₂/moisture release) are located at the broad end of the egg.
  2. The air cell is located at the broad end of the egg.
  3. The depth of air cell in a freshly laid egg is 1–3 mm (very small; it enlarges with age).

Since the original answer key says 'All the above,' the correct option here specifically addresses the first true statement (as stated in option a).

Egg Structure Quick Reference
  • Egg weight distribution: Albumin 58%, Yolk 31%, Shell + membrane 11%
  • Shell composition: 96% inorganic (CaCO₃, MgCO₃, Ca₃PO₄) + 4% organic
  • Vitelline membrane: separates yolk from albumin
  • Chalazae: twisted albumin strands that keep yolk centred
Air Cell Freshness Test
  • Fresh egg (1–3 mm air cell) → sinks in water horizontally.
  • 1-week old egg → slightly tilts in water.
  • Old egg (large air cell) → floats vertically or at surface → not suitable for consumption.

posts.post_title: Crude Protein Percentage in Typical Broiler Ration
posts.post_content: A typical broiler ration contains what percentage of crude protein?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 22–24%

A typical broiler ration contains 22–24% crude protein. Broilers have high protein needs for rapid muscle development and fast body weight gain (market weight at 6 weeks).

Crude Protein Requirements Across Broiler Phases (BIS 2007)
Feed TypeCP% (min.)
Broiler Pre-starter (week 1)23%
Broiler Starter (weeks 2–3)22%
Broiler Finisher (weeks 4–6)20%
Typical broiler ration (overall)22–24%
Why Broilers Need More Protein Than Layers
  • Broilers grow from ~40 g (day-old chick) to ~2 kg in just 6 weeks — rapid muscular development demands high protein.
  • Layers need less body protein; energy goes into egg production instead.
  • Broiler FCR = 2 (2 kg feed needed per kg weight gain).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 18–20% → insufficient for maximum broiler growth performance.
  • 16–18% → this is the crude protein range for layer rations.
  • 12–16% → too low; used for layer grower or certain maintenance rations.

posts.post_title: Germinal Disc Diameter: Fertile vs Infertile Egg
posts.post_content: The diameters of the germinal disc in a fertile egg and an infertile egg are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4.5 mm (fertile) & 3.5 mm (infertile)

The germinal disc of a fertile egg is larger (4.5 mm diameter) compared to an infertile egg (3.5 mm diameter). This size difference can be used to identify fertilisation status of an egg.

Blastoderm vs. Blastodisc
  • Blastoderm (fertile egg): 4.5 mm diameter; appears as a white disc with a clearly defined outer ring — because fertilization has occurred and cells have divided to form a multi-layered blastoderm.
  • Blastodisc (infertile egg): 3.5 mm diameter; appears as a small white spot without a clear ring — no fertilization has occurred.
Memory Tip

Blastoderm (fertilised) = Disk is Depth (bigger, 4.5 mm). Blastodisc (infertile) = smaller disc (3.5 mm).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 3.5 mm & 4.5 mm → reversal of the correct order (fertile is larger, not smaller).
  • 6.5 mm & 5.5 mm → overestimate; actual diameters are 4.5 mm and 3.5 mm.
  • 4.5 mm & 5.5 mm → the infertile egg cannot be larger than the fertile one.

posts.post_title: Function of Vitelline Membrane in Egg
posts.post_content: The vitelline membrane of an egg separates:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yolk from albumin

The vitelline membrane is a thin, transparent membrane that surrounds the yolk and separates it from the surrounding albumin (egg white).

Structure of the Egg — Layer by Layer (outside in)
  1. Cuticle (Bloom): Outermost protein layer sealing pores; applied in uterus.
  2. Shell: Hard calcium carbonate layer.
  3. Outer shell membrane
  4. Inner shell membrane (these two membranes together = 11% of egg weight with shell)
  5. Air cell: Between the two shell membranes at broad end.
  6. Albumin (egg white): 4 layers — outer thin, outer thick, inner thin, inner thick (Chalaziferous layer).
  7. Vitelline membrane: Surrounds and separates the yolk from albumin ✔
  8. Yolk: 31% of egg weight.
  9. Germinal disc (Blastoderm/Blastodisc)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Albumin from shell membrane → this is done by the shell membranes themselves (inner and outer).
  • Albumin from egg shell → egg shell surrounds everything; there is no direct membrane between albumin and shell.

posts.post_title: Home Preservation of Eggs — True Statements
posts.post_content: Which of the following is true about home preservation of eggs?

_aimcq_options.text: In water glass method, sodium silicate seals pores of the shell only
In lime water method, Ca(OH)₂ directly seals the pores
Both methods can preserve eggs for 3 months at room temperature

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above (referring to all three correct sub-statements)

All three sub-statements in the original question are true:

  1. Water glass (sodium silicate) method: 1 part sodium silicate dissolved in 10 parts water. The silica deposits and seals the pores of the egg shell, preventing gaseous exchange and microbial entry.
  2. Lime water (Ca(OH)₂) method: Ca(OH)₂ reacts with CO₂ from the egg to form a thin film of CaCO₃ on the shell surface, sealing the pores.
  3. Both methods can preserve eggs at room temperature for approximately 1 month.

posts.post_title: Major Objective of Turning Eggs During Incubation
posts.post_content: The major objective of turning the egg during incubation is:

_aimcq_options.text: It prevents the embryo from sticking to the shell membrane
It prevents the piped egg condition
It ensures uniform temperature distribution in the incubator

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: It prevents the embryo from sticking to the shell membrane

The primary and major objective of turning eggs during incubation is to prevent the developing embryo from adhering (sticking) to the shell membrane. If the embryo sticks, it cannot develop properly and will die.

Turning Protocol
  • Turning is done at 45° vice-versa.
  • At least 8 times per day for optimum hatchability.
  • Done during the first 18 days only (not the last 3 days in the hatcher).
Consequences of Not Turning
  • Embryo sticks to shell membrane → abnormal development → embryo death.
  • High early embryonic mortality.
Position of Egg in Incubator
  • Setter (days 1–18): Upright position (broad end upward).
  • Hatcher (days 19–21): Horizontal position — turning STOPS so the chick can orient itself for pipping (breaking the shell).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Prevents piped egg → piped egg failure is due to low moisture, not lack of turning.
  • Prevents early embryonic death → early embryonic death is due to temperature extremes.
  • Uniform temperature → this is achieved by ventilation fans, not turning.

posts.post_title: Egg Turning Frequency and Duration During Incubation
posts.post_content: During incubation of chicken eggs, turning is done at least ______ times in a day up to ______ days for optimum hatchability:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 8 times, 18 days

For optimum hatchability, eggs should be turned at least 8 times per day during the first 18 days of incubation. Turning is stopped during the last 3 days (days 19–21) when the chick is preparing to hatch.

Why 8 Times Per Day?
  • Each turn is at 45° vice-versa (alternating directions).
  • Minimum of 8 turns = one turn every 3 hours approximately.
  • Modern commercial incubators may turn eggs automatically every hour.
Why Turning Stops After Day 18?
  • After transfer to the hatcher tray, eggs are placed horizontally.
  • The chick needs to orient its head toward the air cell (broad end) for internal pipping.
  • Turning during this phase disturbs the chick and can cause malposition → dead-in-shell.
Critical Incubation Parameters Summary
  • Temperature (Days 1–18): 37.5–37.6°C | (Days 19–21): 37.2°C
  • Humidity (Days 1–18): 60% R.H. | (Days 19–21): 70% R.H.
  • O₂: 21% | CO₂: max 0.5%
  • Turning: 8 times/day, days 1–18 only

posts.post_title: Days of Candling During Chicken Egg Incubation
posts.post_content: During incubation of chicken eggs, candling by electric candler in a dark room is done on:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 7th & 18th day of incubation

Candling is performed twice using an electric candler in a dark room:

  • 1st Candling: 7th day — to discard infertile eggs (clear/transparent appearance with no embryonic development visible).
  • 2nd Candling: 18th day — to discard dead-in-shell eggs (dark, opaque mass with no movement).
What Each Candling Reveals
  • Fertile egg (7th day): Spider-web appearance of blood vessels; embryo visible as a dark spot with radiating vessels.
  • Infertile egg (7th day): Clear, no blood vessels — discarded to save incubator space and prevent contamination.
  • Blood ring (7th–14th day): Ring of blood visible → indicates early embryonic death.
  • Dead-in-shell (18th day): Dark, opaque mass filling the egg but embryo has died → discarded before transfer to hatcher.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 7th & 14th → second candling is not done on 14th; it is done on 18th (before transfer to hatcher).
  • 14th & 21st → incorrect days for standard candling protocol.
  • 10th & 18th → 10th day is not a standard candling time.

posts.post_title: Purpose of First Candling (Day 7) in Incubation
posts.post_content: During incubation of chicken eggs, the first candling is done on the 7th day to discard:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Infertile eggs

The first candling on the 7th day of incubation is done to identify and discard infertile eggs. By day 7, fertile eggs show clear blood vessel development, while infertile eggs appear clear (transparent) with no development.

Why Infertile Eggs Must Be Removed Early
  • Infertile eggs do not hatch and occupy valuable incubator space.
  • Over time, infertile eggs can become contaminated, develop bacteria, and explode inside the incubator, contaminating other eggs.
Appearance at 1st Candling (Day 7)
  • Fertile egg: Dark embryo (black spot) visible surrounded by a network of blood vessels like a spider-web.
  • Infertile egg: Completely clear, with only the yolk shadow visible — no blood vessels.
  • Early embryonic death (blood ring): A ring of blood visible but no further development — these are also removed.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Dead-in-shell → identified at 2nd candling (18th day).
  • Piped eggs → these are eggs where the chick has started breaking the shell (day 21); not seen during candling.

posts.post_title: Purpose of Second Candling (Day 18) in Incubation
posts.post_content: During incubation of chicken eggs, the 2nd candling is done on the 18th day to discard:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dead-in-shell

The second candling on the 18th day of incubation is done to discard dead-in-shell eggs before the eggs are transferred from the setter tray to the hatcher tray. At this stage, dead-in-shell eggs appear as a dark, opaque mass with no embryo movement.

Dead-in-Shell Condition
  • Cause: Poor ventilation (low O₂ / high CO₂) and/or faulty turning of eggs.
  • Appearance at candling: Completely dark/opaque without any movement or blood vessel pulsation.
  • Why remove before hatcher? If left in the hatcher, dead-in-shell eggs can burst or rot and contaminate live, healthy eggs.
Comparison of Two Candlings
CandlingDayPurpose
1st7th dayDiscard infertile eggs
2nd18th dayDiscard dead-in-shell eggs
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Piped eggs → these are hatching eggs found on day 21; not discarded during incubation.
  • Infertile eggs → already removed at 1st candling on day 7.

posts.post_title: Blood Ring on Candling — What It Indicates
posts.post_content: A blood ring seen during candling of a chicken egg indicates:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Early embryonic death

A blood ring seen during candling is a ring of blood visible just inside the shell, indicating that the embryo started developing (blood vessels formed) but then died early. This is pathognomonic of early embryonic death.

What Causes Early Embryonic Death?
  • Extreme temperatures in the incubator (too high or too low).
  • Nutritional deficiencies in the breeder hen (especially Vit. A, B₂, E, Mn).
  • Disease or infection in the breeder flock.
Candling Appearances Summary
  • Infertile egg: Clear, transparent — no blood vessels, only yolk shadow.
  • Blood ring: Ring of collapsed blood vessels → early embryonic death ✔
  • Fertile, live egg (day 7): Spider-web of vessels; dark embryo spot.
  • Dead-in-shell (day 18): Dark, opaque mass; no movement; embryo died late.
  • Piped egg: Air cell has been broken by chick's beak; visible crack from inside.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Infertile egg → appears clear, not as a blood ring.
  • Piped egg → is a late-stage event (day 21) visible externally; not seen as blood ring.
  • Dead-in-shell → appears as dark opaque mass, not a ring of blood.

posts.post_title: Scalding Temperature-Time for Broiler
posts.post_content: Scalding temperature-time combination for broiler should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 58°C / 1 min

Scalding is the process of immersing birds in hot water to loosen feathers before plucking. For broilers, the standard scalding temperature-time is 58°C for 1 minute.

Scalding Temperature Comparison
  • Broiler: 58°C / 1 min (lower temperature because broiler skin is tender)
  • Layer: 60°C / 1 min (slightly higher temperature needed to loosen tougher, older skin)
Poultry Processing Steps (in order)
  1. Slaughter (Halal with stunning is preferred commercially)
  2. Scalding – immersion in hot water to loosen feathers
  3. Picking/De-feathering – removal of feathers
  4. Singing – passing carcass over blue flame for 5–10 seconds to burn hair-like appendages
  5. Eviscerating – removal of internal organs
  6. Chilling/Storage – chilled dressed chicken stored at 2°C for up to 7 days
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 60°C / 1 min → this is the scalding protocol for layers, not broilers.
  • 62°C / 1 min → too high for broilers; would damage the skin.
  • 65°C / 1 min → excessively high; causes skin tearing and discolouration.

posts.post_title: Best Commercial Method for Egg Preservation
posts.post_content: An excellent method for commercial preservation of eggs is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cold storage method

The cold storage method is the most excellent and widely used method for commercial preservation of large numbers of eggs.

Cold Storage Method Details
  • Temperature: 14°C with 90% Relative Humidity.
  • Oil-coated eggs: Can be preserved for up to 8 months.
  • Non-oil-coated eggs: Can be preserved for up to 6 months.
  • Oil coating seals the shell pores, preventing moisture loss and microbial entry.

  • Pasteurization → used for liquid/broken-out eggs, not whole shell eggs.

posts.post_title: Scalding Temperature-Time for Layer
posts.post_content: Scalding temperature-time combination for layer should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 60°C / 1 min

For layers (older birds with tougher skin), the scalding temperature-time combination is 60°C for 1 minute. A slightly higher temperature than broilers is needed because layers have denser, tougher feather follicles.

Scalding Temperature Comparison
  • Broiler: 58°C / 1 min
  • Layer: 60°C / 1 min ✔
Types of Scalding
  • Soft/Slack scalding: 50–54°C, used when the skin is to be kept intact (e.g., New York dressed birds).
  • Semi-scalding: 58–60°C (the standard commercial range).
  • Hard/Subscalding: 65–68°C, used for waterfowl (ducks, geese) where feathers are harder to remove.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 58°C / 1 min → this is for broilers, not layers.
  • 62°C / 1 min → exceeds required temperature; may damage skin quality.
  • 65°C / 1 min → hard scalding range; used for waterfowl, not layers.

posts.post_title: Duration of Cold Storage for Oil-Coated Eggs
posts.post_content: In the cold storage method of egg preservation, oil-coated eggs can be preserved for ______ months at 14°C and 90% R.H.:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 8 months

In cold storage at 14°C and 90% R.H., oil-coated eggs can be preserved for up to 8 months.

Why Oil Coating Extends Shelf Life
  • Egg shell has 7,500–17,000 pores through which CO₂ and moisture escape and microorganisms can enter.
  • Oil (mineral oil) applied to the shell seals these pores, slowing moisture loss and preventing bacterial contamination.
  • This extends cold storage life from 6 months (non-oiled) to 8 months (oiled).
Comparison: Oil-Coated vs. Non-Oil-Coated in Cold Storage
TypeTemperatureR.H.Duration
Oil-coated eggs14°C90%8 months
Non-oil-coated eggs14°C90%6 months
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 4 months → insufficient; oil-coated eggs last longer.
  • 6 months → this is the duration for non-oil-coated eggs.
  • 12 months → exceeds even the extended oil-coated shelf life.

posts.post_title: Precursor of Niacin
posts.post_content: The precursor of Niacin (Vitamin B₃) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tryptophan

Tryptophan is the metabolic precursor of Niacin (Vitamin B₃). In poultry and mammals, 60 mg of Tryptophan is required to synthesize 1 mg of Niacin. This conversion is, however, very inefficient.

Why This Matters in Poultry Nutrition
  • Poultry do not synthesize Niacin adequately from Tryptophan at practical dietary levels, so Niacin must be supplemented in the feed.
  • Interestingly, poultry do not require Niacin supplementation from gut bacteria (unlike ruminants), because poultry gut microbiome is limited.
  • Poultry do not require Vitamin C in the feed (can synthesize it), unlike guinea pigs and primates.
Key Vitamin Precursor Relationships
  • Tryptophan → Niacin (Vit. B₃) ✔
  • β-Carotene → Vitamin A
  • 7-Dehydrocholesterol → Vitamin D₃ (by UV light)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Tyrosine → precursor of thyroid hormones, melanin, and catecholamines; not Niacin.
  • Phenylalanine → precursor of Tyrosine; not directly linked to Niacin.
  • Methionine → sulphur-containing amino acid; no direct link to Niacin synthesis.

posts.post_title: Duration of Cold Storage for Non-Oil-Coated Eggs
posts.post_content: In the cold storage method of egg preservation, non-oil-coated eggs can be preserved for ______ months at 14°C and 90% R.H.:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 6 months

In cold storage at 14°C and 90% R.H., non-oil-coated eggs can be preserved for up to 6 months.

Why Non-Oiled Eggs Have a Shorter Shelf Life
  • Without oil coating, the pores of the egg shell remain open.
  • CO₂ gradually escapes → albumin pH rises → albumin quality deteriorates (lower Haugh unit).
  • Moisture is lost over time → weight loss of egg increases → air cell enlarges.
  • Microorganisms can potentially penetrate through unblocked pores.
Quality Deterioration Indicators Over Storage
  • Decreasing Haugh unit (albumin quality falls).
  • Decreasing yolk index (yolk flattens).
  • Increasing air cell size.
  • Rising internal pH of albumin.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 4 months → unnecessarily short; non-oiled eggs at proper cold storage last 6 months.
  • 8 months → this is the duration for oil-coated eggs, not non-oiled ones.
  • 12 months → exceeds the shelf life even for oil-coated eggs.

posts.post_title: Site of Fertilization in Poultry
posts.post_content: The site of fertilization in poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Infundibulum

In poultry, the site of fertilization is the Infundibulum. This is where the ovum (yolk released from the ovary) is collected and fertilized by spermatozoa within approximately 15 minutes of ovulation.

Comparison: Fertilization Sites
  • Mammals (e.g., cow, sheep): Fertilization occurs in the Ampulla of the fallopian tube.
  • Poultry (hen): Fertilization occurs in the Infundibulum of the oviduct.

posts.post_title: Poultry Capital of India
posts.post_content: Which state is known as the Poultry Capital of India?

Andhra Pradesh is known as the Poultry Capital of India. It contributes the highest share of egg and broiler production in the country.

Key Poultry Research Institutions in India
  • CARI (Central Avian Research Institute): Izatnagar, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh — the apex institution for poultry research in India.
  • DPR (Directorate of Poultry Research): Rajendra Nagar, Hyderabad, Telangana.

posts.post_title: Perosis — Nutrient NOT Responsible
posts.post_content: Perosis (Slipped tendon) in poultry is NOT caused by deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thiamine (Vit. B₁)

Perosis (Slipped tendon / Hock disease) is a leg disorder in poultry characterised by enlargement of hock joint and displacement of gastrocnemius tendon. It is caused by deficiency of Mn, Biotin, Choline, Folic acid, and Niacin. Thiamine (Vit. B₁) is NOT involved in causing Perosis.

Thiamine (Vit. B₁) Deficiency Disease
  • Polyneuritis — characterised by star-gazing posture (opisthotonus) in poultry; retraction of head backward.
Complete List of Nutritional Deficiency Diseases in Poultry
  • Vit. A: Nutritional roup (nasal discharge, eye discharge)
  • Vit. B₁ (Thiamine): Polyneuritis (star-gazing / opisthotonus)
  • Vit. B₂ (Riboflavin): Curled toe paralysis (penguin-like posture)
  • Vit. E: Crazy chick disease / Encephalomalacia
  • Vit. D: Rickets in chicks; Cage layer fatigue in layers
  • Biotin: Fatty Liver Kidney Syndrome (FLKS)
  • Mn / Choline / Biotin / Folic acid / Niacin: Perosis (Slipped tendon) ✔
  • Zn: Swollen hock syndrome
  • Mo: Femoral head necrosis
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Mn, Choline, Biotin → all are genuine causes of Perosis; so the question asks which is NOT a cause, and the answer is Thiamine.

posts.post_title: Linoleic Acid Requirement for Maximum Egg Size in Laying Hen
posts.post_content: Linoleic acid requirement for a laying hen for maximum egg size should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1%

The linoleic acid (LA) requirement for a laying hen for maximum egg size is 1% of the diet. This is also confirmed by the BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) 2007 standards for layer feed.

Linoleic Acid in Poultry Nutrition
  • Linoleic acid (18:2, ω-6) is the essential fatty acid for poultry.
  • It is essential for: normal growth, feathering, egg production, and maximum egg size.
  • The BIS 2007 standard specifies: minimum 1.0 g/100 g feed (= 1%) for all layer phases.
  • Deficiency leads to: reduced egg size, poor feathering, growth depression.
Essential Fatty Acid and Essential Amino Acid for Poultry
  • Essential fatty acid: Linoleic acid
  • Essential amino acid: Glycine (most critical for poultry; unlike mammals where it is non-essential)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 2%, 3%, 5% → exceed the established minimum requirement; the BIS-specified minimum is 1%, which is sufficient for maximum egg size.

posts.post_title: Maximum Fish Meal Level in Pig Feed to Avoid Fishy Flavour
posts.post_content: Fish meal should not be fed at a level higher than ______% in pig feed, as otherwise a fishy flavour may develop in pork:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10%

Fish meal should not be fed at a level higher than 10% in pig (swine) feed; exceeding this level imparts a fishy flavour to pork, making it commercially unacceptable.

Why Fishy Flavour Develops
  • Fish meal contains trimethylamine oxide (TMAO), which is reduced to trimethylamine (TMA) by gut bacteria. TMA is then deposited in tissues and fat, causing the characteristic fishy odour/flavour.
  • This problem is especially pronounced in pigs because of their monogastric digestive system and fat deposition pattern.
Fish Meal Usage Guidelines in Animal Feeds
  • Poultry: Fish meal can be included up to 5–8% in starter rations and reduced in finisher rations to avoid flavour carry-over in eggs and broiler meat.
  • Pigs: Maximum limit is 10%; beyond this, pork quality is compromised.
  • Fish meal is an excellent protein supplement — contains 60–65% crude protein and rich in lysine, methionine, and available phosphorus.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 5% → unnecessarily restrictive; 10% is the established practical limit.
  • 15%, 20% → too high; fishy flavour would definitely be a problem at these levels.

posts.post_title: Optimum Shell Thickness for Best Hatching
posts.post_content: Optimum shell thickness for best hatching result in chicken eggs is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 0.33 mm

The optimum egg-shell thickness for the best hatching result is 0.33 mm. This allows adequate gaseous exchange (O₂ in / CO₂ out / H₂O out) through the shell pores while maintaining structural integrity for the developing embryo.

Shell Thickness and Hatching
  • Shell that is too thin (< 0.30 mm): excessive moisture loss, poor structural support → weak chick or embryo death.
  • Shell that is too thick (> 0.50 mm): impedes gas exchange and makes pipping (breaking out) difficult for the chick → dead-in-shell.
  • Each egg has approximately 7,500–17,000 pores; maximum pores are at the broad end (where the air cell and embryo head form).
Note on Question 101 vs 109
  • Q101 — Range for standard quality egg: 0.30–0.50 mm
  • Q109 — Optimum for best hatching: 0.33 mm (specific value within that range)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 0.22 mm → too thin; gaseous exchange would be excessive, leading to desiccation of the embryo.
  • 0.43 mm → within acceptable range but not the optimum for hatching.
  • 0.50 mm → at the upper limit; can impede pipping and gas exchange.

posts.post_title: Match the Column: Poultry Terminology
posts.post_content:
Match the following poultry terminology with the correct definitions:

TABLE-ITABLE-II
1. Phallus(a) Unproductive layer
2. Capon(b) Male fowl under 1 year of age
3. Pullet(c) Heat source for brooding
4. Cockerel(d) Penis of fowl
5. Hover(e) Castrated male fowl
6. Loaffer(f) Female chicken laying for the 1st time

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-d, 2-e, 3-f, 4-b, 5-c, 6-a

The correct matches are:

  • 1. Phallus → (d) Penis of fowl: Phallus is the reproductive organ (penis) of the male fowl. Used in vent sexing (Japanese method) to identify male chicks.
  • 2. Capon → (e) Castrated male fowl: A capon is a surgically or chemically castrated male chicken, raised for meat; has more tender flesh.
  • 3. Pullet → (f) Female chicken laying for the 1st time: A pullet is a young female chicken that has just started laying eggs (typically around 22 weeks of age).
  • 4. Cockerel → (b) Male fowl under 1 year of age: A cockerel is a young male chicken less than one year old. After one year, it becomes a Cock/Rooster.
  • 5. Hover → (c) Heat source for brooding: A hover is the brooding equipment that provides supplemental heat to day-old chicks during the brooding period (0–8 weeks).
  • 6. Loaffer → (a) Unproductive layer: A loaffer (loafer) is a hen that is not laying eggs — an unproductive bird that should be culled.
Complete Poultry Terminology Quick Reference
  • Layer: Poultry raised for egg production
  • Broiler/Fryer: Young chicken up to 8 weeks, raised for meat
  • Roaster: Young chicken 12–16 weeks, heavier than broiler
  • Clutch: Batch of eggs laid on consecutive days
  • Cock/Rooster: Adult male fowl (≥1 year)

posts.post_content: The egg stays for the maximum time in which part of the oviduct?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

The egg spends the maximum time in the Uterus — approximately 21 hours. This is where the hard shell, shell pigments, and cuticle are deposited over the egg.

Infundibulum15 minCollects yolk; fertilization
Magnum3 hoursSecretes albumin
Isthmus1 hr 15 minSecretes shell membranes
Uterus21 hoursSecretes shell, pigments, cuticle
Vagina—Holds egg until oviposition

Total time for egg formation = 24–26 hours (length of the ovulatory cycle).

Why the Uterus Takes So Long
  • Shell formation is a complex mineralisation process: calcium carbonate crystals are deposited layer by layer around the egg.
  • The hen must mobilise large amounts of calcium from medullary bone and dietary sources every day.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Infundibulum → only 15 minutes (fertilization and yolk pickup).
  • Isthmus → 1 hr 15 min (shell membrane deposition).
  • Magnum → 3 hours (albumin deposition; longest AFTER uterus, but still shorter).

posts.post_title: Water Quality Standards for Poultry
posts.post_content: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding water quality for poultry?

_aimcq_options.text: Safe upper limit for salt in drinking water for poultry is 3,000 ppm
Safe upper limit of fluoride in water is 2 ppm
Water containing 1,000 ppm TDS is good for poultry

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three statements about poultry water quality standards are correct.

Water Quality Standards for Poultry
ParameterSafe/Acceptable Limit
Salt (NaCl) in drinking water≤ 3,000 ppm (safe upper limit)
Fluoride in water≤ 2 ppm

Consequences of Poor Water Quality
  • Excess salt (>3,000 ppm): Wet droppings, diarrhoea, reduced feed intake, salt toxicity.
  • Excess fluoride (>2 ppm): Fluorosis — bone and beak malformations, reduced production.
  • High TDS (>3,000 ppm): Considered unfit for poultry — reduces water intake, poor health and production.
Note

Compare with feed salt: maximum salt in poultry feed is 0.5% (5,000 ppm) as per BIS 2007, but in drinking water the limit is 3,000 ppm due to the large volumes of water consumed daily.

posts.post_title: Energy Requirement Unit for Poultry
posts.post_content: Energy requirement of poultry is expressed in terms of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: ME (Metabolizable Energy)

Energy requirement of poultry is expressed in terms of Metabolizable Energy (ME), measured in kcal/kg of feed.

Why ME for Poultry?
  • Poultry excrete both urine and faeces together through the cloaca as urine-faecal mix — making it impossible to measure faecal and urinary energy losses separately.
  • ME = GE − (Faecal energy + Urinary energy)
  • Since faecal + urinary are excreted together in poultry, ME is the most practical energy measure.
Energy Measures for Different Species

PigsDE (Digestible Energy)
Ruminants (cattle, sheep)ME or NE (Net Energy)
ME Values from BIS 2007 (Poultry Feed)
  • Broiler prestarter: 3000 kcal/kg
  • Broiler starter: 3100 kcal/kg
  • Broiler finisher: 3200 kcal/kg
  • Layer Phase I: 2600 kcal/kg; Layer Phase II: 2400 kcal/kg

posts.post_title: Effects of Poor Ventilation in Poultry House
posts.post_content: Poor ventilation in poultry house may cause:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

Poor ventilation in a poultry house leads to multiple harmful consequences simultaneously, affecting both the birds and the litter quality.

Effects of Poor Ventilation
  • Accumulation of CO (Carbon Monoxide): Produced by incomplete combustion from gas brooders or heaters in poorly ventilated houses. CO is toxic even at low concentrations.
  • Accumulation of NH₃ (Ammonia): Ammonia is produced from the microbial decomposition of uric acid in poultry litter (faeces + bedding). The maximum permissible limit of NH₃ in a poultry house is 25 ppm. Above this level, it causes respiratory distress, eye damage (keratoconjunctivitis), and increased susceptibility to respiratory diseases like Chronic Respiratory Disease (CRD).
  • Wet litter condition: Without adequate airflow, moisture from bird respiration and droppings cannot evaporate, leading to wet, caked litter. Wet litter promotes coccidiosis, bumblefoot, breast blisters, and ammonia build-up.
Safe Gas Levels in Poultry House
  • NH₃ maximum: 25 ppm
  • CO₂ maximum: 3,000 ppm (0.3%)
  • CO should ideally be zero

posts.post_title: Egg White Injury Factor
posts.post_content: Egg white injury factor is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Avidin

Avidin is the egg white injury factor. It is a glycoprotein present in raw egg white that binds biotin (Vitamin B₇) with extremely high affinity, preventing its absorption and causing biotin deficiency.

Mechanism of Egg White Injury
  • Avidin in raw egg white irreversibly binds dietary biotin in the intestine.
  • This prevents biotin absorption → Biotin deficiency → Fatty Liver Kidney Syndrome (FLKS) in poultry, and dermatitis/hair loss in other animals.
  • Cooking (heat) denatures avidin → cooked egg white does NOT cause biotin deficiency.
Anti-Nutritional Factors in Egg White
FactorAction
AvidinBinds Biotin → Biotin deficiency (Egg White Injury)
OvomucoidTrypsin inhibitor → reduces protein digestion
ConalbuminIron chelating (binds iron, reducing its availability)
LysozymeAntibacterial (actually protective — not harmful)

posts.post_title: Water Glass Used for Egg Preservation
posts.post_content: Water glass used for egg preservation is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sodium Silicate

Water glass is the common name for Sodium Silicate (Na₂SiO₃). It is used in the water glass method of home egg preservation by sealing the pores of the eggshell.

How It Works
  • Eggs are immersed in a solution of 1 part sodium silicate in 10 parts water.
  • Silica from sodium silicate seals the pores of the eggshell, preventing entry of air and microorganisms, and loss of moisture and CO₂.
  • Eggs can be preserved for approximately 1 month at room temperature by this method.

posts.post_title: Maximum Permissible NH₃ Limit in Poultry House
posts.post_content: Maximum permissible limit of NH₃ in poultry house should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 25 ppm

The maximum permissible limit of ammonia (NH₃) in a poultry house is 25 ppm. Above this level, it causes significant health problems in birds.

Effects of High NH₃ Levels
  • Respiratory tract irritation: Damages the epithelial lining, increasing susceptibility to Chronic Respiratory Disease (CRD), caused by Mycoplasma gallisepticum.
  • Eye damage (Keratoconjunctivitis): Blindness, eye ulcers.
  • Reduced growth and production: Feed intake and egg production decline.
  • Wet litter: Ammonia and wet litter go hand-in-hand — wet litter produces more ammonia.
How to Control NH₃ in Poultry Houses
  • Ensure adequate ventilation.
  • Add superphosphate or hydrated lime to litter at 0.5 kg per 15 sq ft of floor space.
  • Turn litter at least once weekly.
  • Maintain litter depth at 8–12 inches (deep litter system).

posts.post_title: Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) for Broiler Chicken
posts.post_content: Feed conversion ratio (FCR) for a broiler chicken should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2

The standard Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) for broiler chicken is 2, meaning 2 kg of feed is required to produce 1 kg of live body weight.

Understanding FCR
  • FCR = Total Feed Consumed ÷ Total Live Weight Gain
  • A lower FCR is better (fewer kg of feed per kg of meat produced).
  • Broiler FCR of 2 means: total feed (3.8 kg) ÷ live weight gain (~1.9 kg) ≈ 2.
Factors Affecting FCR
  • Feed quality (energy and amino acid density)
  • Health status (disease reduces FCR efficiency)
  • Genetics (commercial broiler strains have been selectively bred for better FCR)
  • Environmental temperature (cold = more energy for heat, worse FCR; hot = reduced feed intake)
FCR in Context
SpeciesApproximate FCR
Broiler chicken2.0
Pig3.0
Beef cattle6–8

posts.post_title: Definition of Giblet in Poultry
posts.post_content: Giblet is the carcass of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gizzard, Liver & Heart

Giblet refers to the edible offal package of a poultry carcass, comprising the Gizzard, Liver, and Heart. These are typically packaged inside the dressed carcass cavity for retail sale.

Composition of Giblets
  • Gizzard (Ventriculus/Muscular stomach): The largest single organ in poultry. Its inner lining contains 'koilin', a tough protein layer. The gizzard grinds ingested food.
  • Liver: Large, dark red/brown bilobed organ. Rich in Vitamin A, iron, and B vitamins.
  • Heart: Muscular organ with high protein content.
Poultry Carcass Terms
  • Dressed carcass: After slaughter, bleeding, scalding, defeathering, and evisceration.
  • Giblets are always sold separately or packed inside the carcass.
  • Chilled dressed chicken can be stored for 7 days at 2°C.

posts.post_title: Chemical Used for Fumigation of Poultry House
posts.post_content: Chemical used for fumigation of poultry house is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: KMnO₄ & Formalin

The standard fumigant for poultry houses is a combination of Potassium Permanganate (KMnO₄) and Formalin (Formaldehyde solution).

Fumigation Procedure
  • The reaction between KMnO₄ and formalin produces formaldehyde gas, which is a potent broad-spectrum disinfectant that destroys bacteria, viruses, fungi, and spores.
  • The poultry house is closed and sealed for several hours after fumigation.
  • Fumigation is done between flocks to reduce pathogen load before introducing new chicks.
Ratio Used
  • Per 2.83 m³ (100 cubic feet) of space: 35 mL formalin + 17.5 g KMnO₄ (or as recommended)
  • The formalin is placed in a ceramic/clay container first; KMnO₄ is added second (the reaction is exothermic and releases gas immediately).
Safety Note

Formaldehyde is toxic to humans and birds. The house must be properly ventilated before re-entry and before chick placement (minimum 24–48 hours after fumigation).

posts.post_title: Average Weight of Newborn Chicken Chick
posts.post_content: Average weight of a newborn chicken chick is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 18 g

The average weight of a newly hatched chicken chick is 18 g. This is approximately 1/3 of the standard egg weight (58 g), as approximately 2/3 of the egg mass is used for embryonic development and evaporative water loss during incubation.

Weight Comparison
  • Standard chicken egg weight: 58 g
  • Newborn chick weight: ~18 g (approximately 31% of egg weight)
  • Egg weight at 22 weeks (start of laying): 36 g
  • Egg weight at 42 weeks (peak production): 58 g (standard/mature size)
Egg Size Classification
  • Jumbo egg: more than 70 g
  • Standard egg: 58 g
  • Small/Pee-wee egg: less than 40 g

posts.post_title: Best Layer Breed of Chicken
posts.post_content: Best layer breed of chicken is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Leghorn

White Leghorn is the best layer breed in the world. It belongs to the Mediterranean breed group (origin: Italy) and is the foundation breed for all commercial layer hybrids globally.

Why Leghorn is the Best Layer
  • Average egg production of improved White Leghorn strain: 300 eggs/year.
  • Lays white-shelled eggs (all Mediterranean breeds lay white eggs).
  • Standard body weight: cock 2.7 kg, hen 2.0 kg (lightweight = less feed for body maintenance, more energy for eggs).
  • Characteristics of a good layer breed: alert temperament, lack of broodiness, late moulting.

posts.post_title: Breed with Purple Comb, Wattles and Tongue
posts.post_content: Purple coloured comb, wattles and tongue are characteristics of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kadaknath

Kadaknath is a unique Indian breed found in the Jhabua and Dhar districts of Madhya Pradesh. It is characterized by a completely black (melanistic) phenotype — including purple/black comb, wattles, tongue, skin, bones, and meat.

Special Features of Kadaknath
  • Also known as Kalamasi (meaning 'fowl with black flesh').
  • Has maximum disease resistance among poultry breeds.
  • Its meat has aphrodisiac properties (believed to stimulate sexual desire) — hence high commercial/medicinal value.
  • Lightest poultry breed in the world: cock = 1.5 kg, hen = 1.0 kg.
  • Used primarily for medicinal purposes.
Compare: Aseel
  • Aseel has a small pea comb, bright red wattles and earlobes (not purple).
  • Aseel is an Indian fighting/meat breed from Andhra Pradesh, UP, and Rajasthan.
  • Standard weight: cock 4.5 kg, hen 3.5 kg.

posts.post_title: Calcium Level in Broiler and Layer Feed
posts.post_content: Percent calcium level in broiler and layer feed should be respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1% & 3–3.5%

As per BIS 2007 standards:

  • Broiler feed: Calcium minimum = 1% (for all phases: prestarter, starter, finisher)
  • Layer feed: Calcium minimum = 3.0% (Phase I) to 3.5% (Phase II)
Why Layers Need Much More Calcium
  • The eggshell is composed of 96% inorganic matter, of which 94% is calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
  • Each egg shell contains approximately 2 g of calcium.
  • A laying hen producing 300 eggs/year needs a continuous supply of calcium for shell formation.
  • Calcium deficiency in layers causes soft-shelled eggs and osteoporosis (cage layer fatigue).
Phosphorus Levels (BIS 2007)
  • Broiler: 0.7% (all phases)
  • Layer Phase I: 0.65%, Layer Phase II: 0.65%

posts.post_title: Vitamin Not Synthesized in Poultry
posts.post_content: Which vitamin is NOT synthesized in poultry?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vitamin C

Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid) is NOT synthesized in poultry and must be supplemented in the diet under stress conditions. It is also notably absent in eggs, meat, and milk.

Vitamin C in Poultry
  • Under normal non-stressful conditions, poultry can synthesize Vitamin C in the kidney and liver (unlike humans who lack L-gulonolactone oxidase).
  • However, under heat stress, disease stress, or high production phases, the synthesis is inadequate and supplementation is needed.
  • Poultry generally do NOT require Vitamin C in the feed under normal conditions — hence it is listed as 'not required in feed' from a dietary supplementation standpoint.
Other Vitamins Not Required in Poultry Feed
  • Niacin (Vitamin B₃): Generally NOT required in poultry feed because it can be synthesized from tryptophan (precursor) in poultry.
  • All other vitamins (A, D, E, K, B1, B2, B6, B12, Biotin, Folic acid, Pantothenic acid) must be supplied in the diet.

posts.post_title: Vitamin Generally Not Required in Poultry Feed
posts.post_content: Generally, poultry do NOT require which vitamin in the feed?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Niacin

Poultry generally do NOT require Niacin (Vitamin B₃) in the feed because it can be synthesized endogenously from the amino acid tryptophan, which is its precursor.

Tryptophan → Niacin Conversion
  • 60 mg of tryptophan is converted to approximately 1 mg of Niacin.
  • As long as the diet provides adequate tryptophan, poultry can meet their Niacin needs.
  • This is why Niacin is not listed as a dietary requirement in standard poultry feed formulations.
Niacin Deficiency (when it occurs)
  • Deficiency causes Perosis (slipped tendon / black tongue in poultry) — though Perosis is more typically linked to Mn, Biotin, Choline, and Folic acid deficiency.
  • In practice, corn-based diets (low in tryptophan) may require Niacin supplementation.
Note on Vitamin C

Vitamin C is also NOT required under normal conditions (synthesized by poultry), but Niacin is the textbook answer for this question based on the answer key of the Animal Science Refresher.

posts.post_title: Age for Debeaking and Marek’s Disease Vaccination
posts.post_content: Age of Debeaking and Marek's disease vaccination in chicken is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1 day old

Both debeaking (beak trimming) and Marek's disease vaccination (HVT-MD vaccine) are performed at day-old chick stage (1 day of age).

Debeaking
  • Debeaking prevents cannibalism and feather pecking.
  • Done at day-old using a hot blade that cuts and cauterizes the beak tip simultaneously.
  • The upper beak is cut slightly shorter than the lower beak.
Marek's Disease Vaccination
  • HVT (Herpesvirus of Turkey) vaccine is the most commonly used live vaccine against Marek's disease.
  • Administered subcutaneously or in ovo at day-old.
  • Marek's disease is caused by a herpesvirus that causes neural and visceral tumours (lymphoma).
Other Age-Specific Management
  • Dubbing (removal of comb, wattles, earlobes): Done at 3-day-old chick stage.

posts.post_title: Average Egg Production of Improved White Leghorn Strain
posts.post_content: The average egg production of an improved strain of White Leghorn is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 300 eggs/year

An improved strain of White Leghorn can produce approximately 300 eggs per year. This makes it the world's most productive layer breed.

Leghorn Key Facts
  • Origin: Leghorn, Italy (Mediterranean breed group)
  • Egg shell colour: White
  • Body weight: Cock = 2.7 kg, Hen = 2.0 kg
  • Character: Nervous, active, non-broody — ideal for egg production
  • All commercial layer hybrids are derived from White Leghorn.
Production Timeline
  • Egg production starts at 22 weeks of age.
  • Peak production at 32–35 weeks (~85% production rate).
  • Birds are replaced at 72 weeks.
  • Total eggs in one laying cycle: approximately 280–320 eggs.

posts.post_title: Term for Removal of Comb, Wattles and Earlobes in Poultry
posts.post_content: Removal of comb, wattles and earlobes in poultry is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dubbing

Dubbing is the surgical removal of the comb, wattles, and earlobes in poultry. It is performed at 3 days of age in chicks.

Purpose of Dubbing
  • Reduces frostbite damage to the comb and wattles in cold climates.
  • Reduces injuries from fighting (especially in game birds like Aseel).
  • Reduces the energy expended in maintaining blood circulation to these large appendages in cold weather.
Related Poultry Management Terminology
  • Debeaking: Removal of part of the beak to prevent cannibalism and feather picking; done at day-old.
  • Culling: Removal of unproductive, sick, or inferior birds from the flock.
  • Docking: Tail removal — applicable in other livestock (dogs, pigs), not a standard poultry term.
  • Caponization: Castration of male fowl → produces a Capon (castrated male fowl).

posts.post_title: Most Essential Nutrient in Poultry Feed
posts.post_content: The most essential nutrient in poultry feed is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Water

Water is the most essential nutrient in poultry feed and overall nutrition. Even brief periods of water deprivation cause rapid and significant drops in egg production and body weight.

Why Water is Most Essential
  • Water makes up approximately 65–70% of the body weight of poultry.
  • A standard chicken egg contains 74% water.
  • Water regulates body temperature (evaporative cooling via panting — poultry do not sweat).
  • A layer hen needs approximately 200–300 mL of water per day.
  • Deprivation of water for just 24 hours can take 2–3 weeks of production recovery.
Water Quality Standards
  • Safe upper limit of salt in drinking water: 3,000 ppm
  • Safe upper limit of fluoride: 2 ppm
  • TDS ≤ 1,000 ppm considered good quality
  • Daily water requirement for 100 hens: 20–30 litres

posts.post_title: Age of Dubbing in Poultry
posts.post_content: Age of Dubbing in poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3 day old chick

Dubbing (removal of comb, wattles, and earlobes) is done when chicks are 3 days old. At this age, the tissues are soft and small, making the procedure quick and less stressful than at a later age.

Why at 3 Days?
  • At 3 days, the comb and wattles are rudimentary (tiny) — easy to snip with surgical scissors with minimal bleeding.
  • Older birds have a larger, more vascular comb — dubbing causes more bleeding and stress.

posts.post_title: Light Colour Used to Control Cannibalism in Poultry
posts.post_content: The colour of light used to control cannibalism in poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Red

Red light is used to control cannibalism and feather pecking in poultry. Under red light, blood from wounds appears dark/invisible, reducing the stimulus for other birds to peck at injured birds.

Why Cannibalism Occurs
  • Poultry are attracted to the colour red — wounds, prolapsed tissue (vent), or blood-stained feathers trigger pecking by other birds.
  • Primary cause: Fibre-free diet (diet should contain 3–4% crude fibre).
  • Other causes: overcrowding, boredom, nutritional deficiencies, bright white light.
Management Strategies to Control Cannibalism
  • Use red light (wounds not visible under red light).
  • Debeaking at day-old age.
  • Ensure adequate fibre in diet.
  • Reduce stocking density.
  • Provide adequate feeders and waterers (competition triggers aggression).

posts.post_title: Number of Baby Chick Drinkers for 250 Chicks
posts.post_content: How many baby chick drinkers should be provided for brooding management of 250 chicks?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

For one brooding unit of 250 chicks during the 1st week of age, 4 baby chick waterers (drinkers) are required.

Standard Brooding Unit Specifications

  • Heating: Four 60-watt bulbs hanging at 6-inch height
  • Brooder guard: 5 feet radius
  • Feeders (1st week): 3 egg-tray feeders
  • Waterers (1st week): 4 baby chick waterers
