posts.post_title: Salt Concentration in Poultry Feed (BIS Standard)
posts.post_content: As per BIS, the salt concentration in poultry feed should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 0.5%

As per BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) 2007, the maximum permissible salt (NaCl) concentration in poultry feed is 0.5% for all types of poultry rations — from broiler prestarter to layer Phase II.

Why Salt is Limited
  • Poultry are highly sensitive to excess salt (NaCl). Salt toxicity causes: excessive thirst, wet droppings, diarrhoea, and in severe cases, death.
  • Poultry have no ability to efficiently regulate sodium excretion — unlike mammals.
Salt-Related Standards for Poultry
  • Salt in feed (max): 0.5% (BIS 2007 — applies to all poultry feed types)
  • Salt (NaCl) in drinking water (safe upper limit): 3,000 ppm
  • Tibial dyschondroplasia: High dietary level of chloride (not sodium) may increase its incidence in broilers.

posts.post_title: Maximum Eggs Hatched by a Broody Hen
posts.post_content: Maximum number of eggs that can be hatched by a broody hen is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 15 eggs

A broody hen can hatch a maximum of 15 eggs at a time. This is limited by the physical coverage area of a hen's body.

Natural vs. Artificial Incubation
  • Broody hen (natural incubation): Can incubate up to 15 eggs; best coverage for uniform heat and turning.
  • Artificial incubator: Commercial incubators can hold thousands of eggs with uniform temperature, humidity, and mechanical egg turning.
Broodiness in Poultry
  • Broodiness is the maternal instinct to sit on and incubate eggs.
  • It is a sex-linked trait controlled by the hormone Prolactin.
  • Good layers (e.g., Leghorn) show less broodiness — energy is directed toward egg production, not incubation.
  • Indigenous breeds (desi hens) are the best mothers for natural hatching.
  • Broodiness interrupts egg production — the bird stops laying while sitting on eggs.

posts.post_title: Maximum Weight Loss During Incubation of Chicken Egg
posts.post_content: Maximum weight loss during incubation of a chicken egg is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 12.6%

During the entire 21-day incubation period, a chicken egg loses a maximum of 12.6% of its initial weight through evaporation of moisture via the pores of the eggshell.

Why Weight Loss Occurs
  • The egg loses water vapour through its ~8,000 pores continuously during incubation.
  • This weight loss is controlled by maintaining proper relative humidity in the incubator: 60% RH during days 1–18 and 70% RH during the last 3 days.
  • Too much weight loss (>15%) → chick dehydration and failure to hatch.
  • Too little weight loss (<10%) → excess fluid, drowned chick in shell.
Relationship to Air Cell
  • As the egg loses moisture, the air cell (at the broad end) grows in size.
  • The depth of the air cell in a freshly laid egg is only 1–3 mm.
  • By day 18, the air cell should occupy approximately 1/3 of the egg — the chick will pip into the air cell before external pipping.

posts.post_title: Breeding Birds Needed to Fill a 1000-Egg Incubator
posts.post_content: A 1000-egg capacity incubator would need how many breeding birds to keep it full?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 125

To keep a 1,000-egg capacity incubator fully loaded, you would need 125 breeding birds.

The Rule

The number of layers (breeding hens) required = 1/8th of the total egg capacity of the incubator.

Calculation: 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 breeding hens

Why 1/8?
  • A chicken egg takes 21 days to incubate.
  • A commercial incubator is loaded in batches — a new batch is added every 3 days (setter holds eggs for 18 days; hatcher holds for last 3 days).
  • With eggs loaded every 3 days over 21 days, there are approximately 7 batches in the incubator at any time.
  • To supply ~143 eggs every 3 days, and given ~85% production rate, approximately 125–130 hens are needed.

posts.post_title: Period During Which Chicken Eggs Are Turned in Incubator
posts.post_content: Turning of the chicken egg during incubation should be done:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: During first 18 days only

Eggs in the incubator are turned only during the first 18 days of incubation (in the setter). During the last 3 days (in the hatcher), turning is stopped and eggs are placed horizontally to allow the chick to position itself correctly for pipping and hatching.

Turning Details
  • Angle of turning: 45° vice-versa (alternate direction)
  • Frequency: At least 8 times per day for optimum hatchability
  • Objective: To prevent the embryo from sticking to the shell membrane
What Happens If Turning Is Stopped in the Last 3 Days?
  • The chick begins to position its head under the right wing toward the air cell (broad end).
  • It pips into the air cell first (internal pip), then breaks through the shell (external pip).
  • Continuing to turn during the last 3 days would disorient the chick and cause failed hatching (piped egg condition).

posts.post_title: Daily Water Requirement for 100 Hens
posts.post_content: Daily water requirement for 100 hens is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 20–30 litres

The daily water requirement for 100 laying hens is 20–30 litres, meaning approximately 200–300 mL (about 0.2–0.3 litres) per hen per day.

Water Quality Standards for Poultry
  • Safe upper limit of salt (NaCl) in drinking water: 3,000 ppm
  • Safe upper limit of fluoride in water: 2 ppm
  • TDS (Total Dissolved Solids) ≤ 1,000 ppm is considered good quality water for poultry.
Importance of Water in Poultry
  • Water is the most essential nutrient for poultry. Even brief water deprivation rapidly reduces egg production.
  • An egg is approximately 74% water, and laying hens need adequate water for egg formation.
  • Brooding management: 4 waterers per brooding unit of 250 chicks (1st week); 4–6 waterers from 2nd to 4th week.

posts.post_title: Total Feed Requirement of a Broiler (0–6 Weeks)
posts.post_content: Total feed requirement for a broiler during its whole life (0–6 weeks) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3.8 kg

The total feed consumed by a broiler chicken during its entire production life of 0 to 6 weeks is approximately 3.8 kg.

Feed Consumption Summary
  • Broiler (0–6 weeks): 3.8 kg total
  • Layer (21–72 weeks): 40 kg total
  • Layer per day: 110 g
Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) for Broiler
  • FCR of broiler = 2 (i.e., 2 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of live weight)
  • Good FCR for commercial broilers is around 1.8–2.0
  • Market weight of broiler at 6 weeks: approximately 1.5–2.0 kg
Broiler Ration Requirements (BIS 2007)
  • Prestarter (1st week): 23% CP, ME 3000 kcal/kg
  • Starter (2nd–3rd week): 22% CP
  • Finisher (4th–6th week): 20% CP
  • Calcium: 1% for all broiler phases

posts.post_title: Total Feed Requirement During Laying Period
posts.post_content: Total feed requirement during laying period (21–72 weeks) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 40 kg

During the full laying period from 21 to 72 weeks of age, a layer hen consumes a total of approximately 40 kg of feed.

Calculation Basis

  • Daily consumption: 110 g/day
  • Total = 357 × 110 g ≈ 39.27 kg ≈ 40 kg
Layer Ration Requirements (BIS 2007)

High calcium (3–3.5%) is essential in layer diets for proper egg shell formation (shell = ~94% calcium carbonate).

posts.post_title: Light Requirement for Layers
posts.post_content: Light requirement for a layer is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 16 hours

Layers require 16 hours of light per day for optimum egg production. The remaining 8 hours are in darkness.

Light Requirements Across Poultry Types
  • Layer: 16 hours of light/day
  • Broiler: 23 hours of light/day (near-continuous light to maximize feed intake and growth)
Why Light Matters for Layers
  • Light stimulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, triggering LH and FSH release which drives ovulation and egg production.
  • Light should never be decreased during the laying period, as this signals the approaching winter and suppresses production.
  • Recommended light intensity for layers: 10 lux at bird level.
  • Red light is used to control cannibalism and feather pecking in poultry.

posts.post_title: Daily Feed Requirement of a Layer
posts.post_content: Feed requirement for a layer per day is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 110 g

The standard daily feed requirement for a laying hen (layer) is 110 g per bird per day.

Feed Requirements at a Glance
  • Layer per day: 110 g
  • Broiler total (0–6 weeks): 3.8 kg
  • Layer total (21–72 weeks): 40 kg
  • Daily water requirement for 100 hens: 20–30 litres
Why This Matters

Accurate feed allowance is essential for maintaining optimal body weight, peak egg production, and egg quality. Underfeeding reduces egg size and production; overfeeding increases feed costs and fat deposition. The layer ration must contain 16–18% crude protein and 3–3.5% calcium for shell formation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 100 g — insufficient; would lead to reduced production and body weight loss.
  • 120 g and 140 g — excess amounts; not the standard recommendation for commercial layers.

posts.post_title: Light Requirement for Broilers
posts.post_content: Light requirement for a broiler is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 23 hours

Broilers require 23 hours of light per day. This near-continuous lighting encourages more feed consumption, maximizing daily weight gain and achieving market weight (1.5–2 kg) within 6 weeks.

Why Near-Continuous Light for Broilers?
  • Broilers are raised purely for rapid meat production. Light keeps them active and eating for more hours per day.
  • 1 hour of darkness per day is maintained as a precaution: if a power failure occurs, birds that have never experienced darkness may panic and pile up (smothering death). The 1-hour dark period acclimatizes them.
Light Summary
Poultry TypeLight HoursPurpose
Layer16 hoursStimulate ovulation & egg production
Broiler23 hoursMaximize feed intake & growth rate

posts.post_title: Effect of O₂ Drop on Hatchability
posts.post_content: For every 1% drop in the O₂ content of an incubator, the hatchability will drop by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5%

For every 1% fall in O₂ level below the optimum of 21% in the incubator, hatchability drops by 5%. Similarly, every 1% rise in O₂ above 21% raises hatchability by 5%.

Incubator Gas Requirements
  • Optimum O₂ level: 21%
  • Optimum CO₂ level: 0.5%
CO₂ Rules
  • Every 1% rise in CO₂ above 0.5% → increases embryonic mortality.
  • If CO₂ rises above 5% for a prolonged period → all embryos die, hatchability = 0%.
Temperature is Most Critical

Among all incubation factors, temperature is the most critical factor. The optimum temperature during days 1–18 is 37.5°C (99.5°F), and 37.2°C during the last 3 days (hatcher). Even 1–2°C deviation can cause embryonic death or malformations.

posts.post_title: Best Method for Large-Scale Chicken Slaughter
posts.post_content: Which method is better for slaughtering chicken on a large scale?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Halal with stunning

For large-scale commercial chicken slaughter, Halal with stunning is the preferred method. Stunning (usually electrical stunning) renders the bird unconscious before slaughter, minimizing pain and stress, while the Halal cut ensures complete blood drainage (bleed-out), which is essential for meat quality and shelf life.

Why This is the Best Method
  • Animal welfare: Stunning eliminates suffering during slaughter.
  • Meat quality: Complete blood drainage (from Halal throat cut) prevents blood retention in tissues, reducing microbial load and extending shelf life.
  • Commercial efficiency: Stunned birds are easier and safer to handle on automated processing lines.
Slaughter & Processing Steps
  1. Stunning → Bleeding (Halal cut) → Scalding → Defeathering (Picking) → Singeing → Evisceration → Chilling → Packaging

Chilled dressed chicken can be stored for 7 days at 2°C.

posts.post_title: Essential Fatty Acid and Amino Acid for Poultry
posts.post_content: Essential fatty acid and essential amino acid for poultry are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Linoleic acid & Glycine

For poultry, the essential fatty acid is Linoleic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid, 18:2) and the essential amino acid is Glycine.

Why Linoleic Acid?
  • Linoleic acid cannot be synthesized by poultry and must be supplied in the diet.
  • Requirement for laying hens for maximum egg size: 1% of the diet.
  • As per BIS 2007, minimum linoleic acid in layer feed = 1.0 g/100g feed.
  • Deficiency causes reduced egg size, poor hatchability, and fatty liver.
Why Glycine?
  • Glycine is conditionally essential for poultry — birds cannot synthesize it at rates adequate for maximum growth.
  • It is required in large amounts for feather protein (keratin) synthesis and as a conjugate for uric acid excretion (birds excrete nitrogen as uric acid, unlike mammals).
  • Glycine + Serine are together considered essential for optimal poultry performance.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Arachidonic acid — essential for cats, not poultry.
  • Lysine — important amino acid for poultry but it is the first limiting amino acid in cereal-based diets, not the designated 'essential' amino acid in this context.
  • Linolenic acid (18:3, omega-3) — not the primary essential FA for poultry.

posts.post_title: Storage Temperature for Chilled Dressed Chicken
posts.post_content: Chilled dressed chicken can be stored for 7 days at a temperature of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2°C

Chilled dressed chicken (fresh, non-frozen) can be stored safely for 7 days at 2°C. This temperature is just above freezing but low enough to significantly retard microbial growth.

Poultry Meat Storage at Different Temperatures
  • 2°C (Chilled/Refrigerated): 7 days for dressed chicken
  • −18°C or below (Frozen): Several months to 1 year
Poultry Processing — Temperature–Time for Scalding
  • Broiler scalding: 58°C for 1 minute (soft scalding — feathers removed easily without skin damage)
  • Layer scalding: 60°C for 1 minute (harder scalding needed due to tougher skin)
Singeing

After defeathering, carcasses are passed over a blue flame for 5–10 seconds to burn off remaining hair-like pin feathers (singeing).

posts.post_title: Longest Part of Poultry Oviduct
posts.post_content: The longest part of the poultry oviduct is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Magnum

The Magnum is the longest part of the poultry oviduct, measuring 38 cm in length, and the egg spends 3 hours here during which albumin (egg white) is secreted.

Note: Although the egg stays the longest time in the Uterus (21 hours), the Magnum is the physically longest segment at 38 cm.

posts.post_title: Diseases Against Which Broilers Are Vaccinated
posts.post_content: The broiler is commonly vaccinated against:

_aimcq_options.text: Marek's disease, Chicken pox, Gumboro, Ranikhet

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Marek's disease, Ranikhet & Gumboro

Broilers are routinely vaccinated against only three viral diseases: Marek's disease, Ranikhet (Newcastle Disease), and Gumboro (Infectious Bursal Disease — IBD).

About Each Disease
  • Marek's disease: Caused by a herpesvirus; causes tumours of nerves and organs (lymphoma); vaccine (HVT — Herpesvirus of Turkey) given at day-old chick.
  • Ranikhet (Newcastle Disease): Highly contagious; caused by Avian paramyxovirus type-1; causes respiratory, nervous, and digestive signs; F1 strain vaccine used.
  • Gumboro (IBD): Caused by a birnavirus; destroys the Bursa of Fabricius causing immunosuppression; the bursa is the B-lymphocyte maturation organ in birds.
Note on Fowl Pox

Fowl pox vaccination is done in layers, not routinely in broilers (because broilers have a short production life of only 6 weeks, and pox takes longer to be a significant risk).

posts.post_title: Secretion of Egg Components in Poultry Oviduct
posts.post_content: Egg yolk, albumin and shell membranes of the chicken egg are respectively secreted by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ovary, Magnum, Isthmus

Each component of the egg is produced by a specific organ or oviduct segment:

  • Egg yolk: Formed in the Ovary. The yolk (ovum) matures in the follicle of the ovary and is released (ovulation) into the infundibulum. The characteristic yellow colour of egg yolk is due to Carotene (xanthophyll pigments).
  • Albumin (Egg white): Secreted by the Magnum over about 3 hours. The magnum is the longest oviduct segment (38 cm). Albumin contains ovomucoid (trypsin inhibitor), conalbumin (iron chelating), lysozyme (antibacterial), and avidin (biotin-binding — raw egg white injury factor).
  • Shell membranes: Secreted by the Isthmus in about 1 hour 15 minutes. There are two shell membranes — inner and outer — which together with the shell form about 11% of the total egg weight.
Memory Aid

O-M-I-U-V → Ovary (yolk), Magnum (albumin), Isthmus (shell membranes), Uterus (shell + pigment + cuticle), Vagina (oviposition)

posts.post_title: Incubation Period of Japanese Quail
posts.post_content: Incubation period for Japanese quail egg is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 17 days

The incubation period for the Japanese quail (Coturnix coturnix japonica) egg is 17 days — the shortest among commonly farmed poultry species.

Why Quail?

Quail have the shortest generation interval among poultry. They start laying at 6–7 weeks of age, making them ideal for research and rapid commercial production. Their eggs weigh only about 10 g (standard).

posts.post_title: Haugh Unit Range for Standard Chicken Egg
posts.post_content: Range of Haugh unit for a standard chicken egg should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 65–80

The Haugh unit of a standard chicken egg ranges from 65 to 80 (some sources cite 65–85, with the standard value being 72). It is the primary measure of albumin (egg white) quality.

What is Haugh Unit?
  • Haugh unit measures the height of the thick albumin relative to the egg weight.
  • Higher Haugh unit = better, fresher egg quality (thicker, firmer albumen).
  • As eggs age, the albumin thins due to enzymatic breakdown of ovomucin, and the Haugh unit falls.
  • Standard chicken egg Haugh unit: 72 (range 65–85).
Egg Quality Measures
ParameterWhat It MeasuresStandard Value
Haugh unitHeight of albumin (albumin quality)72 (range 65–85)
Yolk indexSpherical nature of yolk (yolk quality)0.50 (range 0.40–0.50)
Egg Shape Index (ESI)Shape of egg (width/length × 100)74 (for chicken)

posts.post_title: Chalaziferous Layer of Albumin
posts.post_content: A chalaziferous layer of albumin is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inner thick layer

The chalaziferous layer is the inner thick layer of albumin that directly surrounds the yolk and holds it in a central position via the chalazae (twisted cord-like structures).

Four Layers of Egg Albumin (from outside to inside)
  1. Outer thin layer — fluid, watery consistency
  2. Outer thick layer — gel-like; major volume of albumin
  3. Inner thin layer — fluid layer just outside the chalaziferous layer
  4. Inner thick layer (Chalaziferous layer) — dense; forms twisted chalazae that anchor the yolk centrally; maintains yolk position during incubation
Function of Chalazae
  • The chalazae are rope-like structures formed from the chalaziferous layer that twist in opposite directions and anchor the yolk at the centre of the egg.
  • In fresh eggs, chalazae are prominent and firm. In stale eggs, they break down and the yolk can move freely.
  • Chalazae are a quality indicator: well-defined chalazae = fresh egg.

posts.post_title: Haugh Unit and Yolk Index — What They Measure
posts.post_content: Haugh unit and yolk index of the egg are respective measures of:

_aimcq_options.text: Width of albumin & Elliptical nature of yolk
Height of albumin & Spherical nature of yolk
Depth of albumin & Circular nature of yolk

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Height of albumin & Spherical nature of yolk
  • Haugh unit measures the height of the thick albumin after breaking an egg on a flat surface. A taller albumin mound = higher Haugh unit = better quality. Standard value = 72 (range 65–85).
  • Yolk index measures the spherical nature of the yolk. Formula: Yolk Index = Yolk Height ÷ Yolk Width. Standard value = 0.50 (range 0.40–0.50). A fresh yolk is round and stands high (yolk index close to 0.50); a stale yolk flattens out (yolk index falls).
Why These Values Decrease with Age

As eggs age, the enzyme lysozyme breaks down ovomucin in the albumin, causing the thick white to liquefy (albumin height drops → Haugh unit falls). Similarly, the vitelline membrane weakens over time, causing the yolk to flatten (yolk index decreases). Both are therefore direct indicators of egg freshness.

Instruments Used for Egg Quality Measurement
  • Haugh unit: Tripod micrometer / spherometer
  • Yolk index: Ruler / micrometer after egg break-out
  • Egg Shape Index: Vernier caliper
  • Shell thickness/strength: Screw gauge
  • Specific gravity: Brine flotation technique

posts.post_title: Age of Peak Egg Production in Layers
posts.post_content: Peak egg production in a layer is at the age of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 32–35 weeks

Peak egg production in a commercial layer is achieved at 32–35 weeks of age, at which point approximately 85% production is observed.

Egg Production Cycle of a Laying Hen
PhaseAge PeriodKey Events
Phase I22–42 weeksProduction rises from 0 to peak (~85%); egg size increases from 36 g to 58 g
Phase II43–62 weeksEgg production declines to ~65%
Phase III63–72 weeksProduction below 65%; layer replaced at 72 weeks
Key Production Facts
  • Egg production starts at 22 weeks (5.5 months of age).
  • After peak, production declines at 0.5% per week.
  • Layers are replaced at 72 weeks (18 months) of age.
  • Average egg production of improved White Leghorn strain: 300 eggs/year.

posts.post_title: Best Feeding Method to Avoid Selective Feeding
posts.post_content: To avoid selective feeding, the best method of poultry feeding for commercial production is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All mash feeding

All mash feeding is the best method to prevent selective feeding in commercial poultry production. In this method, all feed ingredients are uniformly ground and mixed into a homogeneous mash, leaving no opportunity for birds to pick and choose specific ingredients.

Comparison of Feeding Methods
MethodSelective Feeding RiskComments
Whole grain feedingMaximum — birds pick and choose grainsOldest method; highest selectivity
Grain & mash feedingModerateSlightly better than whole grain
All mash feedingMinimum — uniform mix prevents selectionBest for all types of commercial housing
Pellet feedingMinimal but pellets are expensiveReduces wastage; 10% more costly than mash
Key Point

Selective feeding leads to nutritional imbalance, as birds tend to prefer high-energy, palatable ingredients and avoid others. All mash feeding ensures uniform nutrient intake per bird.

posts.post_title: Function of Cloaca in Poultry
posts.post_content: The cloaca is a common opening for:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Digestive, urinary and reproductive systems

The cloaca is a single common chamber that connects to — and serves as the common exit for — the digestive, urinary, and reproductive tracts in poultry. It opens to the outside through the vent.

Structure of Cloaca
  • Coprodeum: receives faeces from the large intestine.
  • Urodeum: receives urine from the ureters and eggs/sperm from the reproductive tract.
  • Proctodeum: the final chamber before the vent; also contains the Bursa of Fabricius (a lymphoid organ important for B-cell maturation in young birds).
Clinical Importance
  • The cloaca is used in the vent sexing (Japanese method) of day-old chicks to differentiate males from females by examining the genital eminence.
  • Cloacal prolapse (tissue protruding from the vent) can trigger cannibalism in flocks — managed using red light which reduces visibility of red-coloured wounds.

posts.post_title: Glandular and Muscular Stomach of Poultry
posts.post_content: Glandular stomach & muscular stomach of poultry are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both A and C (Proventriculus & Gizzard / Proventriculus & Ventriculus)

This question has two correct answers because Gizzard and Ventriculus are the same organ:

  • Glandular stomach = Proventriculus — secretes HCl and pepsinogen for chemical digestion.
  • Muscular stomach = Gizzard = Ventriculus — a thick-walled, muscular organ that physically grinds food. Its inner lining is hardened by koilin secretion.

So option A (Proventriculus & Gizzard) and option C (Ventriculus & Proventriculus) — when reversed — both correctly describe the glandular and muscular stomachs respectively. Hence "Both A & C" is correct.

posts.post_title: Incubation Period for Chicken and Duck
posts.post_content: The incubation period for chicken & duck are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 21 days, 28 days

The incubation period (time from laying to hatching) for major poultry species:

Incubation Periods by Species
  • Domestic fowl (Chicken): 21 days — Gallus domesticus; standard egg weight 58 g
  • Duck: 28 days — Anas platyrhynchos; standard egg weight 70 g
  • Turkey: 28 days — Meleagris gallopavo; standard egg weight 85 g
  • Japanese Quail: 17 days — Coturnix coturnix japonica; standard egg weight 10 g

Larger eggs generally have longer incubation periods. The incubation period is defined as the time from oviposition (egg laying) to hatching of the chick.

posts.post_title: Cause of Early Embryonic Death in Chicken
posts.post_content: The early embryonic death of the chicken embryo is due to:

_aimcq_options.text: Too high or too low temperature in incubator

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Too high or too low temperature in incubator

Early embryonic death (embryo dies in the first few days of incubation) is caused by temperature extremes — either too high or too low.

  • Too high temperature: Accelerates metabolic rate, causing malformations or death in early embryo when it is most vulnerable.
  • Too low temperature: Slows development to a halt; below 21.1°C (physiological zero), embryonic development ceases entirely.
Detection

Early embryonic death is detected by first candling on 7th day. A blood ring seen during candling indicates early embryonic death — the blood vessels have collapsed and the blood has spread in a ring pattern.

posts.post_title: Jumbo Egg Weight Classification
posts.post_content: Chicken egg with more than 70 g weight is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Jumbo egg

Eggs are classified by weight into different grades. A chicken egg weighing more than 70 g is classified as a Jumbo egg — the heaviest commercial grade.

Egg Weight Classification
  • Pee-wee (Undersize): Less than 40 g
  • Peewee/Small: 40–49 g
  • Medium: 50–57 g
  • Standard/Large: 58 g (standard egg used in all quality measurements)
  • Extra Large: 64–70 g
  • Jumbo: More than 70 g
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Pee-wee — the smallest egg category (<40 g), opposite of jumbo.
  • Large sized — a mid-range category, not the >70 g category.
  • Normal egg — not a standard classification term for >70 g eggs.

posts.post_title: Yellow Colour of Egg Yolk
posts.post_content: The characteristic yellow colour of egg yolk is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carotene

The yellow-orange colour of egg yolk is primarily due to carotenoid pigments, particularly carotene (β-carotene) and xanthophylls deposited from the hen's diet.

Important Note
  • Carotene: Responsible for yellow-orange yolk colour — derived from feed (maize, green leaves).
  • Xanthophyll: Also a carotenoid; responsible for yellow colour in skin and shanks of poultry. In some references, xanthophylls also contribute to yolk colour.
  • Riboflavin (Vitamin B2): Responsible for greenish colour in egg white (albumin) — not yolk.
  • Biotin: A B-vitamin involved in fat metabolism, not pigmentation.

Feeding maize (corn) or dried marigold petals enriches yolk colour due to their high carotenoid content.

posts.post_title: Cause of Cannibalism and Feather Picking
posts.post_content: Cannibalism & feather picking in poultry is mainly due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fibre-free diet

Cannibalism (eating of own species) and feather picking in poultry are primarily caused by feeding a fibre-free diet. The recommended crude fiber level in chicken diet is 3–4%.

Why Fibre Matters
  • Adequate dietary fiber keeps birds occupied (longer feeding time).
  • Fibre-free diets lead to boredom, frustration, and redirected pecking behavior.
  • The problem is more common with pelleted and crumbled diets since pellets are consumed quickly, leaving birds with excess time and energy.
Other Contributing Factors
  • Overcrowding
  • Bright white light (solution: use red light)
  • Nutritional deficiencies (protein, sodium)
  • Prevention: debeaking at day-old, using red light, providing adequate space

posts.post_title: Scalding of Poultry During Processing
posts.post_content: Immersing of the birds in hot water for the purpose of loosening of feathers is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Scalding

Scalding is the process of immersing slaughtered poultry in hot water to loosen feather follicles for easier plucking.

Scalding Temperature-Time Standards
  • Broiler: 58°C for 1 minute (softer skin, tender meat)
  • Layer: 60°C for 1 minute (tougher skin requires slightly higher temp)
Poultry Processing Steps (Sequence)
  1. Slaughter (Halal with stunning — preferred commercial method)
  2. Bleeding
  3. Scalding (hot water immersion)
  4. Defeathering/Picking (mechanical plucking)
  5. Singeing (blue flame — burns hair-like filoplumes)
  6. Evisceration
  7. Washing and chilling

posts.post_title: Pee-wee Egg Weight Classification
posts.post_content: Underweight egg (less than 40 g) is generally known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pee-wee egg

An egg weighing less than 40 g is called a Pee-wee egg — the smallest and lightest commercial egg grade.

Egg Weight Classification (Recap)
  • Pee-wee: < 40 g ✔
  • Small: 40–49 g
  • Standard/Large: ~58 g
  • Jumbo: >70 g

Pee-wee eggs are most commonly produced by young pullets at the start of their laying career, when the reproductive system is not yet fully mature. They are generally not sold commercially due to their substandard size.

posts.post_title: Blood Spot in Egg Yolk
posts.post_content: Egg yolk with blood spot is indicative of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemorrhage in ovary & infundibulum

Blood spots in the yolk result from haemorrhage (rupture of blood vessels) at the level of the ovary or infundibulum — the earliest sites of egg formation.

Blood Spot Location Diagnosis
  • Blood spot in yolk: Haemorrhage in ovary or infundibulum (where yolk is collected)
  • Blood spot in albumin (egg white): Haemorrhage in magnum (where albumin is secreted)
Causes of Blood Spots
  • Nutritional deficiency (Vitamin A, K)
  • Genetic predisposition
  • Stress or sudden fright during ovulation
  • Old hens are more susceptible

posts.post_title: Egg Position in Setter and Hatcher
posts.post_content: Position of egg in setter (1st 18 days of incubation) & hatcher (last 3 days of incubation) are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Upright & Horizontal

Egg position in the incubator is critical for proper embryo development:

  • Setter (first 18 days): Eggs placed in upright position — broad end upward. This keeps the air cell (at the broad end) at the top, helping the embryo develop with head positioned toward the air cell.
  • Hatcher (last 3 days): Eggs placed in horizontal position — allows the chick to pip (crack the shell) and hatch freely without rotation constraint.
Why This Matters
  • The air cell at the broad end has maximum pores for gaseous exchange.
  • Head of the embryo forms toward the broad end.
  • Horizontal position in hatcher allows the chick to rotate and pip correctly.

posts.post_title: Singeing of Poultry Carcass
posts.post_content: Passing of carcass over the blue flame for the purpose of burning of hair-like appendages is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Singeing

Singeing is the process of passing the defeathered poultry carcass over a blue gas flame for 5–10 seconds to burn off the fine, hair-like feather appendages called filoplumes that remain after mechanical plucking.

Singeing Details
  • Duration: 5–10 seconds over blue flame
  • Purpose: Removes filoplumes (hair-like pin feathers)
  • Stage in processing: After defeathering/picking, before evisceration
Singeing vs Scalding
  • Scalding: Hot water immersion → loosens feathers for plucking
  • Singeing: Blue flame → burns off residual hair-like filoplumes

posts.post_title: Standard Egg Weight and Energy
posts.post_content: Average weight & energy provided by a standard poultry egg is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 58 g, 90 calorie

The standard chicken egg weighs 58 g and provides approximately 90 calories (kcal) of energy.

Key Nutritional Facts of a Standard 58 g Egg
  • Weight: 58 g
  • Energy: ~90 calories
  • Water content: 74%
  • Dry matter: 26% (protein 13%, fat 11%, carbohydrate 1%, ash 1%)
  • Cholesterol: 230–250 mg
  • Protein: ~13% (whole egg)

The egg is considered one of the most nutritionally complete foods, containing all essential amino acids, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and most B-vitamins (except Vitamin C).

posts.post_title: Blood Spot in Egg Albumin
posts.post_content: Egg albumin with blood spot is indicative of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemorrhage in magnum

When a blood spot is found in the albumin (egg white), it indicates haemorrhage that occurred in the magnum — the part of the oviduct where albumin is secreted.

Blood Spot Diagnosis Summary
  • Blood in yolk → Ovary or infundibulum haemorrhage
  • Blood in albumin → Magnum haemorrhage
Oviduct Sequence (for Reference)
  1. Infundibulum: collects yolk (15 min)
  2. Magnum: secretes albumin (3 hours) ← blood here → blood in albumin
  3. Isthmus: shell membranes (1h 15 min)
  4. Uterus: shell & pigment (21 hours)

posts.post_title: Albumin Secretion Site in Oviduct
posts.post_content: Albumin is secreted by which part of oviduct?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Magnum

The Magnum is the longest part of the oviduct (38 cm) and is responsible for secreting albumin (egg white). The egg spends about 3 hours in the magnum.

Oviduct Parts and Their Contributions
  • Infundibulum (10 cm, 15 min): Collects yolk from ovary; site of fertilization
  • Magnum (38 cm, 3 hours): Secretes albumin (egg white) ✔
  • Isthmus (10 cm, 1h 15 min): Secretes inner and outer shell membranes
  • Uterus (10 cm, 21 hours): Secretes shell, shell pigment, and cuticle
  • Vagina (5 cm): Holds egg until oviposition

posts.post_title: Ovulatory Cycle Length in Hen
posts.post_content: The length of the ovulatory cycle in hen is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 24–26 hours

The ovulatory cycle in a laying hen is 24–26 hours. This is the total time taken from ovulation (release of yolk from ovary) to oviposition (egg laying).

Time Spent in Each Part of Oviduct
  • Infundibulum: 15 minutes (fertilization site; collects yolk)
  • Magnum: 3 hours (albumin/egg white secreted)
  • Isthmus: 1 hour 15 minutes (shell membranes secreted)
  • Uterus: 21 hours (shell, pigment & cuticle secreted)
  • Vagina: Holds until oviposition

Total = ~24–26 hours, which is why a hen lays roughly one egg per day. The hormone Arginine Vasotocin (AVT) from the posterior pituitary triggers oviposition.

posts.post_title: Soft Shelled Eggs Deficiency
posts.post_content: Soft shelled eggs are due to deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium in feed

Soft-shelled or thin-shelled eggs are primarily caused by calcium deficiency in the diet. Eggshell is composed of 96% inorganic matter, of which calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) forms 94%.

Calcium Requirements in Poultry Feed (BIS 2007)
  • Broiler feed: 1% calcium minimum
  • Layer phase I: 3.0% calcium minimum
  • Layer phase II: 3.5% calcium minimum
Eggshell Composition
  • Inorganic matter: 96% (CaCO₃ 94%, MgCO₃ 1%, CaHPO₄ 1%)
  • Organic matter: 4%

Layers need much more calcium than broilers because they deposit ~2 g of calcium into each eggshell. Vitamin D₃ is also critical for calcium absorption — its deficiency can also lead to soft shells.

posts.post_title: Qualities of a Good Layer
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a quality of a good layer?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

All three characteristics are signs of a good layer:

  • Lack of broodiness: Broody hens stop laying to incubate eggs. Good layers like White Leghorn have little or no broodiness. Broodiness is controlled by prolactin hormone.
  • Alertness: Good layers are more active, alert, and easy to handle than poor layers. Temperament is an indicator of laying ability.
  • Late moulting: Late moulters are good layers — they moult briefly (6 weeks from October) and continue laying during the moulting period.
Additional Signs of a Good Layer
  • Early and complete depigmentation (vent first)
  • Large, moist, dilated vent
  • Wide pelvic bones (3+ finger-widths between keel and pubic bones)
  • Pale, dry, shrunken comb in peak laying (due to pigment deposition)

posts.post_title: Guards of Eggs
posts.post_content: Guards of eggs are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

Eggs have natural defense proteins in the albumin that protect against microbial invasion. These "guards" include:

  • Ovomucoid: A trypsin inhibitor — inhibits proteolytic enzymes of invading bacteria and digestive enzymes.
  • Conalbumin (Ovotransferrin): An iron-chelating protein — binds iron, depriving bacteria of this essential mineral for growth.
  • Lysozyme: An antimicrobial enzyme — hydrolyzes the cell wall (peptidoglycan) of bacteria, especially gram-positive organisms.

Together, these proteins form a powerful antimicrobial defense system in the egg white, making the egg naturally resistant to bacterial contamination for some time after laying.

posts.post_title: Egg Within an Egg Condition
posts.post_content: An egg within egg condition is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reverse peristalsis of oviduct

The egg-within-an-egg condition occurs due to reverse peristalsis of the oviduct. In this condition, a fully formed egg is pushed backward (anti-peristalsis) into the upper oviduct, where it becomes engulfed by another developing egg, resulting in an egg inside another egg.

Other Abnormal Egg Conditions
  • Double yolk egg: Two ova released simultaneously or one ovum pushed back when another ovulates.
  • Soft shell: Calcium deficiency.
  • Off-coloured egg / Discoloured yolk: Feeding of cottonseed cake (contains gossypol pigment).
  • Blood spot: Haemorrhage in ovary/infundibulum (yolk) or magnum (albumin).

posts.post_title: Optimum CO₂ and O₂ Concentration in Incubator
posts.post_content: Optimum concentration of CO₂ & O₂ in incubator should be respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 0.5% & 21%

The optimal gas concentrations in a chicken egg incubator are:

  • O₂: 21% — same as normal atmospheric oxygen. For every 1% fall below 21%, hatchability drops by 5%. For every 1% rise above 21%, hatchability rises by 5%.
  • CO₂: 0.5% — the safe threshold. For every 1% rise in CO₂ beyond 0.5%, embryonic mortality rises. If CO₂ exceeds 5% for a prolonged period, all embryos die and hatchability reaches 0%.
CO₂ Levels and Impact
  • 0.5% → Optimum
  • >0.5% → Increasing embryonic mortality
  • >5% prolonged → All embryos dead (hatchability = 0%)

posts.post_title: Early Moulters Laying Capacity
posts.post_content: Early moulters are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Poor layers

Early moulters are poor layers. Moulting is the process of shedding and renewing feathers, during which hens typically stop or reduce egg production.

Comparison: Early vs Late Moulters
  • Early moulters:
    • Poor layers
    • Moulting starts in June–July
    • Moulting completes in 3–4 months (a long break)
    • Do not lay eggs during moulting
    • Should be culled (removed from flock)
  • Late moulters:
    • Good layers
    • Moulting starts in October
    • Moulting completes in just 6 weeks
    • Continue to lay eggs even during moulting
    • Should be retained in flock

posts.post_title: Greenish Colour in Egg White
posts.post_content: The greenish colour in egg white (albumin) is usually due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Riboflavin

Riboflavin (Vitamin B₂) is responsible for the characteristic greenish-yellow tint of egg albumin (egg white). Riboflavin is a yellow-green fluorescent pigment naturally present in egg white.

Egg Colour Chart
  • Yolk yellow/orange: Carotene and xanthophylls
  • Albumin greenish tint: Riboflavin (Vitamin B₂)
  • Darkening of hard-boiled yolk: Iron sulfide (FeS) — from H₂S reacting with iron
  • Skin/shank yellow: Xanthophyll deposited from feed

The riboflavin content of egg white also makes eggs a good dietary source of Vitamin B₂, contributing to energy metabolism and maintenance of mucous membranes.

posts.post_title: Most Critical Factor During Incubation
posts.post_content: Most critical factor during incubation is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Temperature

Temperature is the most critical factor during incubation. Even small deviations from the optimal temperature can cause embryonic death or developmental abnormalities.

Optimal Incubation Temperatures
  • First 18 days (Setter): 37.5°C (99.5°F) — or 37.6°C per some references
  • Last 3 days (Hatcher): 37.2°C (99°F)
Effects of Temperature Deviation
  • Too high temperature: Early embryonic death; malformations
  • Too low temperature: Delayed development; dead-in-shell
  • The physiological zero (temperature at which embryonic growth is arrested) = 21.1°C (70°F)

Other factors (humidity, turning, ventilation) are also important but temperature deviations are most immediately fatal to embryos.

posts.post_title: Order of Moulting in Layers
posts.post_content: Order of moulting in layers (from 1st to last) is:

_aimcq_options.text: Head, neck, breast, body, wings, tail
Head, breast, body, neck, wings, tail
Tail, wings, body, breast, neck, head
Tail, wings, body, neck, breast, head

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Head, neck, breast, body, wings, tail

Moulting in poultry follows a predictable top-to-bottom order, progressing from the head downward to the tail feathers.

Order of Feather Shedding (1st → Last)
  1. Head (first)
  2. Neck
  3. Breast
  4. Body
  5. Wings
  6. Tail (last)

This natural sequence is the same in all chickens. Understanding the order helps poultry farmers identify whether a bird is an early or late moulter, and thereby assess laying quality. Late moulters lose primary wing feathers from the outer to inner direction quickly, and their moulting process is shorter (about 6 weeks), while early moulters take 3–4 months.

posts.post_title: Darkening of Egg Yolk in Hard-Boiled Egg
posts.post_content: Darkening of egg yolk in a hard-boiled egg is due to the formation of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Iron sulfide (FeS)

The dark greenish-grey ring around the yolk of a hard-boiled egg is caused by Iron Sulfide (FeS), which forms when hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) — released from the albumin during overcooking — reacts with iron (Fe) present in the yolk.

Chemical Reaction

H₂S (from albumin) + Fe (from yolk) → FeS (Iron Sulfide) — dark compound

Prevention
  • Do not overcook eggs.
  • Place eggs in cold water immediately after boiling — this stops further H₂S diffusion into the yolk.

The H₂S is generated by the breakdown of sulfur-containing amino acids (cysteine, methionine) in albumin upon heating.

posts.post_title: Albumin Percentage of Egg Weight
posts.post_content: Albumin forms what percentage of the egg weight?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 58%

In a standard chicken egg (58 g), albumin (egg white) constitutes 58% of the total egg weight.

Egg Component Composition (by Weight)
  • Albumin (egg white): 58%
  • Yolk: 31%
  • Shell + shell membrane: 11%
Albumin Layers (4 layers, from outside to inside)
  1. Outer thin layer
  2. Outer thick layer
  3. Inner thin layer
  4. Inner thick layer (Chalaziferous layer — holds yolk in position)

Albumin is a rich source of high-quality protein, riboflavin (Vitamin B₂), and protective proteins (lysozyme, conalbumin, ovomucoid).

posts.post_title: Order of Depigmentation in Layers
posts.post_content: Order of depigmentation in a layer (from 1st to last) is:

_aimcq_options.text: Vent, Eye ring & Earlobes, Beak, Shank

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vent, Eye ring & Earlobes, Beak, Shank

Depigmentation (loss of yellow pigment/xanthophyll) occurs in a specific order in laying hens as egg production continues. The areas with the best blood circulation lose pigment first.

Order of Depigmentation (1st → Last)
  1. Vent (after ~10 eggs) — highest blood flow; depigments first
  2. Eye ring & Earlobes
  3. Beak (after ~25 eggs)
  4. Shank (after ~100 eggs) — lowest blood flow; depigments last

This process is useful for assessing a hen's laying history. Good layers show complete depigmentation. After moulting or cessation of laying, re-pigmentation occurs in the reverse order (shanks repigment first).

posts.post_title: Off-Coloured Egg Production Cause
posts.post_content: Off coloured egg production by a layer is mainly due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Feeding of cotton seed cake

Feeding cotton seed cake (CSC) to layers causes off-coloured eggs, particularly discolouration of the yolk. This is due to gossypol, a toxic polyphenolic pigment naturally present in cottonseed.

Effects of Gossypol on Eggs
  • Yolk discolouration (dark olive-green or mottled)
  • Reduced hatchability
  • Rubbery egg white due to gossypol binding to albumin proteins
Other Cottonseed Cake Effects
  • Can cause cyclopia in chick embryos at high levels
  • Reduces feed palatability
  • The safe level of CSC in poultry feed is limited due to gossypol toxicity

In contrast, maize feeding enhances yolk colour (deepens yellow-orange) due to its high carotenoid content.

posts.post_title: Shell and Shell Membrane Percentage of Egg Weight
posts.post_content: Shell & shell membrane together form what percentage of egg weight?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 11%

The shell and shell membrane together form 11% of the total egg weight in a standard 58 g chicken egg.

Egg Component Breakdown
  • Shell + shell membrane: 11%
  • Albumin (egg white): 58%
  • Yolk: 31%
Shell Composition
  • Inorganic matter: 96% (CaCO₃ = 94%, MgCO₃ = 1%, CaHPO₄ = 1%)
  • Organic matter: 4%

Shell thickness of a standard egg is 0.30–0.50 mm. Optimal shell thickness for best hatching is 0.33 mm. Shell strength is measured using a screw gauge.

posts.post_title: Broodiness and Plumage Traits Classification
posts.post_content: Broodiness, feather growth & colour of plumage are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sex-linked traits

Broodiness, feather growth, and colour of plumage are sex-linked traits in poultry — they are controlled by genes located on the sex chromosomes (Z chromosome in birds).

Understanding Sex-Linked Traits in Poultry
  • Sex-linked traits: Genes located on sex chromosomes (Z/W). Examples: barred plumage, slow/rapid feathering, broodiness.
  • Sex-limited traits: Expressed in only one sex (e.g., egg production in females, milk production in cows).
  • Sex-influenced traits: Expressed differently in each sex (e.g., horn growth in sheep — dominant in males, recessive in females).

In poultry, sex-linked feathering (slow vs. rapid feathering) is used in autosexing — sexing day-old chicks based on feather length without needing vent inspection.

posts.post_title: Match the Column: Poultry Egg Terms
posts.post_content:
Match the column:

TABLE-ITABLE-II
1. Ovomucoid(a) Unproductive layer
2. Yolk index(b) Iron chelating
3. Conalbumin(c) Castrated male fowl
4. Haugh unit(d) Yolk quality
5. Capon(e) Trypsin inhibitor
6. Loaffer(f) Albumin quality

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-e, 2-d, 3-b, 4-f, 5-c, 6-a
  • 1. Ovomucoid → (e) Trypsin inhibitor: Ovomucoid is a glycoprotein in egg white that inhibits trypsin (a proteolytic enzyme), acting as a natural antimicrobial and anti-digestive agent.
  • 2. Yolk index → (d) Yolk quality: Yolk index = Yolk height ÷ Yolk width. Standard range: 0.40–0.50. Measures the spherical (rounded) nature of yolk.
  • 3. Conalbumin → (b) Iron chelating: Also called ovotransferrin; binds iron to deprive bacteria of iron, providing antimicrobial protection.
  • 4. Haugh unit → (f) Albumin quality: Measures the height of egg white; standard value 72 (range 65–85). Higher value = better quality albumin.
  • 5. Capon → (c) Castrated male fowl: Surgical removal of testes in a male chicken to improve meat quality and tenderness.
  • 6. Loaffer → (a) Unproductive layer: A hen that eats feed but does not lay eggs; identified during culling.

posts.post_title: Inorganic and Organic Matter in Eggshell
posts.post_content: Contribution of inorganic & organic matter in egg shell should be respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 96% & 4%

Eggshell is composed of 96% inorganic matter and 4% organic matter.

Eggshell Composition Breakdown
  • Inorganic matter (96%):
    • Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃): 94%
    • Magnesium carbonate (MgCO₃): 1%
    • Calcium phosphate (CaHPO₄): 1%
  • Organic matter (4%): Mainly protein matrix (osteopontin, ovocleidin)

This high inorganic content makes eggshell essentially a calcium carbonate crystal structure, which is why calcium deficiency directly results in soft or thin-shelled eggs. Shell strength is directly proportional to shell thickness (measured by screw gauge).

posts.post_title: Late Moulters Characteristics
posts.post_content: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about late moulters?

_aimcq_options.text: In late moulters, moulting starts in October & completed in 6 weeks
They continue to lay eggs during moulting period

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

All three statements about late moulters are correct:

  • Late moulters are good layers — they produce more eggs over their laying life compared to early moulters.
  • Moulting starts in October and completes in 6 weeks — a very short moulting period, minimizing production loss.
  • They continue to lay eggs during moulting — unlike early moulters who stop production entirely.
Practical Implication

Late moulters should be retained in a commercial flock as they are economically productive. Early moulters (poor layers with long moulting break of 3–4 months) should be culled to improve flock efficiency.

posts.post_title: Most Intensive Type of Poultry Housing
posts.post_content: Most intensive type of poultry housing is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cage system / Battery system

The Cage/Battery system is the most intensive form of poultry housing because it achieves the highest stocking density per unit area, with each bird confined to an individual cage of 14×16 inches floor space and 17 inches height.

Intensity Ranking (Least to Most Intensive)
  1. Free Range / Extensive system (least intensive)
  2. Semi-intensive system
  3. Folding unit system
  4. Deep litter system
  5. Cage/Battery system (most intensive) ✔

The cage system is used exclusively for layer birds. It offers advantages such as better egg hygiene, easy disease monitoring, no litter problems, and reduced cannibalism — but it raises animal welfare concerns.

posts.post_title: Germinal Disc of Fertile vs Infertile Egg
posts.post_content: Germinal disc of fertile egg & infertile egg are respectively known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Blastoderm & Blastodisc
  • Fertile egg: Germinal disc = Blastoderm — a multi-layered disc of cells that has already begun cleavage; diameter ~4.5 mm. Appears as a white ring with clear center under candling.
  • Infertile egg: Germinal disc = Blastodisc — a single-layered disc of cells; diameter ~3.5 mm. Appears as a solid white disc without the ring structure.
Visual Identification
  • Blastoderm (fertile): Bull's eye appearance — white ring with lighter center
  • Blastodisc (infertile): Solid white spot, smaller and uniform

This distinction is important during candling and for selecting fertile eggs for incubation in breeding programs.

posts.post_title: Early Moulter Characteristics
posts.post_content: Which of the following is true about early moulters?

_aimcq_options.text: In early moulters, moulting starts in June–July & completed in 3–4 months
Early moulters do not lay eggs during moulting period

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

All three statements about early moulters are correct:

  • Early moulters are poor layers — low total egg production.
  • Moulting starts in June–July and takes 3–4 months — a long break from laying.
  • They do not lay eggs during moulting — complete cessation of production.
Key Practical Point

Early moulters should be culled early from commercial flocks to reduce feed cost and improve overall flock productivity. Depigmentation pattern and moulting time together help farmers identify poor-performing birds efficiently.

posts.post_title: Litter Depth in Deep Litter System
posts.post_content: The depth of litter material in deep litter system of housing should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 8–12 inches

In the deep litter system, the litter material should be maintained at a depth of 8–12 inches. This depth provides adequate cushioning, insulation, and supports the biological activity that keeps the litter dry and reduces ammonia production.

Deep Litter System Key Facts
  • Litter depth: 8–12 inches
  • Floor space per bird: 3.5–4 sq. ft.
  • Litter materials: Wood shavings, rice husks, sawdust, groundnut hulls
  • Litter turning: At least once weekly
  • To maintain dryness: Superphosphate or hydrated lime @ 0.5 kg per 15 sq. ft.
  • Used for: Both broilers and layers

posts.post_title: Incubation Related Problems
posts.post_content: Which of the following is an incubation related problem?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

All three are recognised incubation-related problems:

  • Early embryonic death: Embryo dies in the first few days — caused by too high or too low temperature, poor quality hatching eggs, or disease in parent flock. Detected by blood ring on candling at 7th day.
  • Piped egg (Pipped): Chick has cracked (pipped) the shell but cannot complete hatching — caused by low humidity/moisture in the hatcher, preventing the chick from rotating and breaking free.
  • Dead-in-shell: Embryo fully develops but dies just before hatching — caused by poor ventilation, faulty turning, or nutritional deficiencies. Detected by 2nd candling on 18th day.

posts.post_title: Commercial Housing System for Poultry
posts.post_content: Commercial housing system of poultry housing is:

_aimcq_options.text: Both deep litter and cage system

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both deep litter and cage system

Both the Deep Litter System and the Cage/Battery System fall under the Intensive housing category, which is the basis of commercial poultry production.

Types of Poultry Housing Systems
  • Free Range / Extensive System: Oldest method; birds roam freely — not commercial.
  • Semi-intensive System: Partially confined — not fully commercial.
  • Folding Unit System: Moveable pens — small scale.
  • Intensive System (Commercial):
    • Deep Litter System: Used for both broiler & layer housing; litter depth 8–12 inches.
    • Cage/Battery System: Most intensive; used for layers only; floor space 14×16×17 inch³ per bird.

posts.post_title: Brooder Temperature and Floor Space in 1st Week
posts.post_content: In Artificial brooder, temperature & floor space requirement per chick during the 1st week of age should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 95°F, 100–120 sq. cm

During the 1st week of brooding, chicks require a brooder temperature of 95°F (35°C) and a floor space of 100–120 sq. cm per chick.

Brooding Temperature and Space Schedule
AgeFloor SpaceTemperature
1st week100–120 cm²/chick95°F
2nd–4th weeks250–300 cm²/chick90°F → 85°F → 80°F
5th–8th weeks700–800 cm²/chick80°F

Temperature is reduced by 5°F each week. One brooding unit consists of 250 chicks, four 60-watt bulbs at 6-inch height, a brooder guard of 5-foot radius, 3 feeders, and 4 waterers.

posts.post_title: Cause of Dead-in-Shell in Chicken Embryo
posts.post_content: Dead-in-shell condition of chicken embryo is due to:

_aimcq_options.text: Both poor ventilation and faulty turning

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both poor ventilation and faulty turning of eggs

The Dead-in-shell condition — where the embryo fully develops but dies just before hatching — is caused by both poor ventilation AND faulty turning of eggs.

  • Poor ventilation: Leads to CO₂ buildup, O₂ depletion — asphyxiation of the embryo in the final stages.
  • Faulty turning: Improper or infrequent turning causes the embryo to stick to the shell membrane, preventing normal positioning for hatching.
Summary of Incubation Problems & Causes
  • Early embryonic death → Too high/low temperature
  • Piped egg (can't hatch) → Low moisture in hatcher
  • Dead-in-shell → Poor ventilation + faulty turning

posts.post_title: Commercial Housing System for Layers
posts.post_content: Commercial housing system used for layer housing is:

_aimcq_options.text: Both deep litter and cage system

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both deep litter and cage system

For layer housing, both the Deep Litter System and the Cage (Battery) System are used commercially.

  • Deep litter system: Floor space 3.5–4 sq. ft. per bird; litter depth 8–12 inches. Suitable for both layers and broilers.
  • Cage/Battery system: The most intensive system; used only for layers (not broilers). Provides 14×16 inches floor space per bird with 17 inch height.

The cage system is preferred in large-scale commercial layer farms for its better egg hygiene, ease of management, and higher stocking density.

posts.post_title: Protein Content of Chicken Meat and Egg
posts.post_content: Average protein content of chicken meat & egg are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 21% & 13%

The average protein content of chicken meat is 21% and of a standard chicken egg is 13%.

Nutritional Composition of Standard 58 g Egg
  • Water: 74%
  • Protein: 13%
  • Fat: 11%
  • Carbohydrate: 1%
  • Ash: 1%
Chicken Meat Composition
  • Protein: ~21%
  • Fat: ~4–10% (varies by cut)
  • Water: ~65–70%

Chicken meat has higher protein per unit weight than egg because egg contains the complete embryonic nutrition package including fat for energy and calcium for shell formation.

posts.post_title: Optimum Temperature and Moisture During Incubation Days 1–18
posts.post_content: Optimum temperature & moisture during 1–18 days of incubation are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 37.5°C & 60% R.H.

During the first 18 days of incubation in the setter:

  • Temperature: 37.5°C (99.5°F)
  • Relative Humidity: 60% R.H.
Incubation Conditions: Setter vs Hatcher
PhaseDaysTemperatureHumidity
Setter1–18 days37.5°C (99.5°F)60% R.H.
Hatcher19–21 days37.2°C (99°F)70% R.H.

Higher humidity in the hatcher helps soften the egg membrane, making it easier for the chick to pip and hatch. Maximum weight loss during incubation is 12.6% of the original egg weight.

posts.post_title: Commercial Housing System for Broilers
posts.post_content: The commercial system used for broiler housing is:

_aimcq_options.text: Both deep litter and cage system

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Deep litter only

For broiler housing, only the Deep Litter System is used commercially. Broilers are not kept in cages.

Why Broilers Use Only Deep Litter?
  • Broilers are meat birds that need more floor space for movement and muscle development.
  • Cage confinement causes breast blisters, leg problems, and poor meat quality in broilers.
  • Deep litter (8–12 inches depth) provides cushioning, comfort, and good litter management for broilers.
Summary Table
  • Broiler housing: Deep litter ONLY
  • Layer housing: Both deep litter AND cage system
  • Cage system: Layers ONLY (not broilers)

posts.post_title: Cholesterol Content of Standard Egg
posts.post_content: Cholesterol content of 58 g standard egg of poultry is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 250 mg

A standard 58 g chicken egg contains approximately 230–250 mg of cholesterol, found almost entirely in the egg yolk. The answer key accepts 250 mg as the standard answer.

Cholesterol Facts
  • Egg yolk is one of the richest dietary sources of cholesterol.
  • All cholesterol is in the yolk; egg white has essentially zero cholesterol.
  • Daily recommended cholesterol intake: <300 mg/day (general population).
  • One egg provides nearly the full daily cholesterol allowance.

Despite high cholesterol content, moderate egg consumption (up to 1 per day) is generally considered safe for healthy adults, as dietary cholesterol has less impact on blood cholesterol than saturated and trans fats for most people.

posts.post_title: Turning Angle of Eggs in Incubator
posts.post_content: Turning of egg in the incubator should be at:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 45° vice-versa

Eggs in the incubator setter should be turned at an angle of 45° in both directions (alternating back and forth) for optimal hatchability.

Turning Details
  • Angle: 45° vice-versa (alternating)
  • Frequency: At least 8 times per day
  • Duration: During first 18 days only (not in the hatcher for the last 3 days)
  • Purpose: Prevents the embryo from sticking to the shell membrane

Modern commercial incubators use automatic turning mechanisms. Manual turning should be done an odd number of times per day so the egg is not in the same position on consecutive nights, which is the most sensitive period for embryo development.

posts.post_title: Chambers of Poultry Stomach
posts.post_content: Poultry stomach is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2-chambered

The poultry (fowl) stomach is 2-chambered, consisting of:

  1. Proventriculus (Glandular stomach): Secretes digestive enzymes and gastric juices. Equivalent to the true stomach in mammals.
  2. Ventriculus / Gizzard (Muscular stomach): The largest single organ in the body. Contains a hard coating called koilin. Its primary function is crushing and grinding of food — serving as teeth for birds.
Comparison with Other Animals
  • Monogastric (1-chambered): Pigs, dogs, horses
  • 2-chambered: Poultry
  • 4-chambered (ruminants): Cattle, buffalo, sheep (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum)

posts.post_title: Process of Egg Laying in Poultry
posts.post_content: The process of egg laying in poultry is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Oviposition

Oviposition is the scientific term for the act or process of egg laying in birds (and other egg-laying animals such as reptiles and insects).

Key Terminology
  • Oviposition: Act of laying an egg
  • Ovulation: Release of ovum (yolk) from the ovary into the infundibulum
  • Incubation: Period from oviposition to hatching
  • Hatching: Emergence of chick from egg

The hormone Arginine Vasotocin (AVT) — secreted by the posterior pituitary — is responsible for uterine contractions that trigger oviposition. The ovulatory-oviposition cycle is approximately 24–26 hours in hens.

posts.post_title: Cause of Piped Egg Condition
posts.post_content: Egg fails to hatch (piped egg condition) is mainly due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Low moisture in incubator

A piped egg is one where the chick has begun to crack the shell (pipping) but fails to complete hatching. This is mainly caused by low moisture (humidity) in the hatcher.

Why Low Moisture Causes Piped Egg
  • Low humidity causes the inner shell membrane to dry out and tighten around the chick.
  • The chick becomes "shrink-wrapped" and cannot rotate to complete the hatching process.
  • Adequate humidity (70% R.H. in hatcher) keeps membranes moist and pliable.
Comparison of Incubation Problems
  • Early embryonic death → Too high/low temperature
  • Piped egg (can't hatch) → Low moisture
  • Dead-in-shell → Poor ventilation + faulty turning
